open brought forward, and an error with no window to say it over
(`open_app_alert`, opened before the window it's about closes, or the
app would end between them). What the windows share is behind a lock
(`Shared`: the search, spelling on or off, the font families, whether
new windows show the ruler and tool bars); one that changes it tells
the hub, which tells them all (`ToHub::Again`). Each window keeps
itself for an upgrade (`save_state`, a `SavedDoc`; `on_upgrade` joins
them), and says while it is saving (`upgrade_waits_while`). A
document's pictures are its own (`Pictures`, decoded on workers that
tell its window). `DocView` keeps the kit's
`editor::Editor` (so a document of any length scrolls and types at full
speed) and is its `EditorHost`, and the `Doc` is its `Document` (`Styled`
in main.rs, which also names each style's font, `fonts::font`): every edit is `Doc::edit`, which moves the
runs: inserted text takes the pending typing style, the style of what it
replaced, or the style before it, and pasting what was copied here
brings its styles back. Undo is our own (snapshots, typing and deleting
coalesced within 2 s); ⌘Z/⌘⇧Z/⌘Y are consumed before the editor sees
them, and what they change goes to the editor with `replaced`. Replace
All splices each match so the styles between them survive. A read-only
document's Font, Paragraph and Document menus are disabled
(`Menu::all_enabled`): its styles are saved with it.

Paragraphs (`doc::Para`, one per paragraph, kept with `para_starts` by
`Doc::splice`): a kind (`Kind`: Body, Title, Heading 1–3, Quote, Code;
choosing one restyles its text, `Kind::apply`, and gives it its space
above and below), a list (bulleted, numbered: `Doc::number` counts its
place among those at its level, deeper ones under it not breaking the
count), an indent level and its own alignment (the Paragraph menu's
Align items set the selected paragraphs'; the document's alignment,
`user.olo.alignment`, is only the default now). Removing text across
paragraphs leaves the first's setting; each newline put in starts a
paragraph set like the one it split, and Return at a heading's end
starts body text. In a list, Return in an empty item steps out a level
(ending the list at the outermost), Tab and ⇧Tab indent it more or less,
Backspace at its start takes its marker away (`Document::key`, which
the editor asks before it acts on those keys). `Doc::format` turns a paragraph into the
editor's `Paragraph` (24 points an indent level, and for a list's
marker, so list text lines up with a quotation's). They are saved in
`user.olo.paragraphs` (JSON, dropped if the count no longer fits the
text), undone with the text, and kept through a reload. The status line
counts words (in the selection too), for documents up to a megabyte.

Tables (`table.rs`): a paragraph's `Para::row` (`doc::Row`: column
shares, header) makes it a table's row, its cells its text between tabs,
so the file itself has the table as tab-separated lines. The Table menu
inserts one (3 by 3, a header row, after the caret's paragraph or in
its place if empty, with a paragraph after it if it would end the
document), converts paragraphs to rows and a table back to text,
toggles the header row, adds rows above or below and columns before or
after, deletes a row, a column or the table, and evens the columns,
each one step to undo (`Doc::replace_paras`: the text change, then the
new paragraphs' settings). Removing text across paragraphs gives the
paragraphs whose newlines are put back their own settings again
(`Doc::splice`), so rows stay rows. Markdown's tables come in as rows
(the head a bold header row), and Word, OpenDocument and RTF tables
too; Export writes them as GitHub tables, `<table>`s, or tables in the
other formats; printing sets each row's cells in their columns, ruled
and kept whole on a page. Columns dragged wider or narrower (a rule,
in the editor) keep their widths in StyledEdit's own files and in Word,
OpenDocument, RTF and HTML (`<colgroup>`); Markdown has no widths.

The ruler (Document ▸ Show Ruler, while lines wrap; each window keeps
its own through a reload, new ones take the last choice) is the
kit's `widgets::ruler::Ruler`, over the text (`Editor::text_span` places it,
and `EditorHost::text_moved` moves it with the text in the same frame): it shows the caret's
paragraph's indents and tab stops, and what is changed on it goes to
every selected paragraph (not a table's rows) as one step to undo, with
a line down the text while a marker is held. `Para::left`, `first` and
`right` are points beyond what the paragraph's kind, level and list
give (`Para::base_indents`; the ruler shows the sums), and `Para::tabs`
its stops (`doc::Tab`), after which a stop every half inch; Code
paragraphs without stops of their own keep a stop every four spaces.
Word, OpenDocument and RTF keep them all (`w:ind`/`w:tabs`;
`fo:margin-left`, `fo:text-indent`, `style:tab-stops` measured from the
indent as LibreOffice has them; `\li`, `\fi`, `\ri`, `\tx` with
`\tqc`/`\tqr`/`\tqdec`; checked in LibreOffice), HTML the indents
(tab stops it hasn't), Markdown neither.

File ▸ Print… (⌘P) shows `olo_print`'s Print panel; Export ▸ PDF… and
the panel's PDF File ask where, then write a PDF. `pages.rs` sets the
document on pages on a worker (with the kit's text system made for it,
`TextSystem::standalone`, and the editor's own layout, so lines break
as in the editor): each paragraph as `Doc::format` sets it, at the
page's text width (an inch's margins), its rows down the pages (a row
that doesn't fit starts the next page; space above isn't kept at a
page's top), each word placed where the layout put it in its own font,
size and colour (justified text stays justified), list markers in the
indent, page numbers at the foot of documents of more than one page.

Pictures (Edit ▸ Insert Picture…, a picture pasted, or a picture file
dropped on the text) are characters: U+FFFC (`editor::PICTURE`) whose
style holds the picture (`doc::Picture`: its file, its size in points,
what it shows), so they flow with the text, are typed around, deleted,
copied, dragged and undone like any letter, and any number go in a
paragraph. `Doc::sections` lays the character out as big as its picture
(`editor::push_picture`: unseen, the row as tall and the glyph as wide),
and the kit's editor draws the picture over it
(`editor::Paragraph::pictures`), a frame while it loads, tinted when
selected. `pictures.rs` decodes each file on a worker (`olo_images`, so
JPEG XL, AVIF and HEIC too, no bigger than 2048 pixels a side) into a
texture. A picture put in is its pixels at 96 to the inch, no wider than
a page's text; Edit ▸ Picture Size fits it to the page or makes it
larger or smaller. In memory a picture's path is absolute; saved, it is
from the document's folder when it's in it, and a picture with no file
of its own (pasted, or from an imported document, held meanwhile in
`~/.cache/olo/styled-edit/pictures`) is copied into a folder beside the
document ("Report pictures" for "Report.txt") as it's saved. Word,
OpenDocument and RTF take each as a picture paragraph of its own
(`olo_richtext::Picture`: a drawing in `word/media`, a frame in
`Pictures/`, a `\pict`; GIF, WebP and the rest made PNGs), and give
theirs back the same way, checked in LibreOffice; a web page holds its
pictures (`data:` addresses), Markdown points at their files
(`![what it shows](path)`, read back from beside the file), and printing
and PDFs place each where its character is (`olo_print::Item::Image`).

Document ▸ Page View (per window, kept through a reload; lines wrap
in it) sets the text on sheets of the paper it prints on
(`olo_print::local_paper`) with the margins it prints with, breaking as
printing breaks (`editor::Pages`); each sheet shows its header and
footer as printed (`pages::margin_lines`), the ruler spans its text.

Document ▸ Header & Footer… sets what every printed page shows in its
margins (`doc::Page`, `Doc::page`): a left, centre and right part of
each, where `{page}` and `{pages}` stand for the page's number and how
many there are (`Page::fill`). Until it's set, pages are numbered at the
foot (so the window starts with `{page}` in the footer's centre); set,
exactly what it says shows, nothing if it's all empty. Each line sits
half way into its margin, in 10-point gray. It is kept in the file's
`user.olo.page` attribute and through a reload, and Word, OpenDocument
and RTF keep it (`olo_richtext::Document::header`/`footer`): Word's
header and footer parts (one paragraph, the parts a centre and a right
tab apart, `PAGE` and `NUMPAGES` fields), OpenDocument's master page
(`text:page-number`, `text:page-count`; its page now with inch margins
like the others) and RTF's `\header`/`\footer` with `PAGE`/`NUMPAGES`
fields; read back from any of them (complex Word fields too), and
checked in LibreOffice. Word's and OpenDocument's files also say tabs
past a paragraph's own stops go every half inch (`w:defaultTabStop`,
`style:tab-stop-distance`), as StyledEdit and RTF have them.

The tool bars (Document ▸ Show Toolbars; each window keeps its own
through a reload, new ones take the last choice) are the kit's
`ToolBar`, cached: along the top New, Open, Save, Print | Undo, Redo |
Cut, Copy, Paste | Find, Check Spelling | Bold, Italic, Underline,
Strikeout | the font, size and colour pickers | the four alignments |
bulleted and numbered lists | indent less and more, in two rows when the
window is narrower than one (the default window fits two); down the left
side Insert Picture, Insert Table, Header & Footer | Page View, Show
Ruler, Wrap Lines. Each tool is the menu command of the same name
(`tool_bars`); the pickers' menus are Font ▸ Size and Color and the
families of the Font menu (`size_menu`, `color_menu`, `families`, shared
with the menus), made from the document as they open.

Spelling is checked as you type (Edit ▸ Check Spelling While Typing,
on); right-clicking a misspelled word offers its suggestions, Ignore
Spelling and Learn Spelling above the Edit commands (`DocWin::spell`).

Other formats (`convert.rs`, on a worker, from a copy of the text, runs
and paragraphs): File ▸ Import… reads a Markdown, Word or
OpenDocument document (Markdown with pulldown-cmark) into a new, untitled one (headings, lists, quotes, code
blocks, bold, italic, struck-out and code text, links with their target
in `Style::link`; a table's rows as lines with tabs between cells, a
rule as a centred `* * *`), so saving it never writes over the source:
a `.md` opened with Open stays its plain text, as it was (people keep
notes in Markdown and edit them as text). File ▸ Export writes a copy as Word,
OpenDocument, Markdown (`to_markdown`: marks hug their text, Markdown's own
characters escaped, a list's items tight, code fenced; sizes, colours
and fonts have no Markdown) or a web page (`to_html`: every style, the
alignment, nested lists), leaving the document where it was. Word,
OpenDocument and RTF (`olo-richtext`, `from_rich`/`to_rich`): Import
reads `.docx`, `.odt` and `.rtf` too (and Open takes them there: they
aren't plain text; their tables come in as tables), and Export writes
any of them, each span's size,
font and colour said, in Olo's font, so they look in Word or LibreOffice
as they do here.

`fonts.rs` owns a font database on a worker thread: it lists families for
the Font menu (in submenus titled like a dictionary's guide words) and
loads a face the first time a style names it, registering it as
`se:Family:R|B|I|BI` with `style::add_document_font`; until then the UI
font stands in. Find and Replace are Haiku's windows (case, wrap-around,
backwards, replace all), shared by every document; ⌘G finds again, ⌘H
finds the selection, ⌘T replaces the same. `save_state` keeps every
window, with unsaved text and styles, its selection and where it was
scrolled to (`Editor::view`), through a reload.

## Activity Monitor (apps/activity)

Everything the machine is doing, in sections down a `Sidebar` (each row
with its figure now): Overview (cards of CPU, memory, network, disks,
GPU and the battery or the hottest sensor, each a way into its section,
and the busiest processes), Processes, Supervisor (what the supervisor
does, below: on or off, each finding as a card with its evidence and
Inspect, Stop Process and Ignore This Process, what it lowered, what it
did lately), CPU (by kind of time, each core
with its frequency, each cluster's frequencies and governor, load),
Memory (with zram's ratio, pressure stall information and every
/proc/meminfo counter), Disks (each disk's traffic, how busy it is, its
requests and their latency; volumes and how full they are; I/O
pressure), Network (each interface's traffic and addresses, the
programs using it most, every connection and its program), GPU (busy, power, memory, and each program's
GPU memory from DRM fdinfo), AI (brush's command model: suggestions
offered and taken, latency, how it learns; HACKING, "brush's
suggestions"), Sensors (the battery's health, cycles and
capacity; the fans against what they cool, below; every temperature
and power sensor), System (the
machine, pressure, and the kernel's tunables, which can be set) and
Graphs (Haiku's ActivityMonitor: graphs of any sources, each scaled to
its own range, from the context menu). ⌘1 to ⌘9 are the sections
(`app_keys`: `activity.overview` and on). Click any graph to look back:
the Overview's last card says what was busiest at that moment (top CPU
and disk processes are kept for each sample, half an hour of them).

It is on olo-kit. The app's looper is a hub (`Hub`, `main.rs`): the
samplers, the helper and the windows tell it things (`Msg`, through
the app's proxy, `tell`), and it keeps who measures, what the app may
do (`Access`, the helper, what's to do once full access comes), the
settings and its windows, each told what it shows. The main window is
the `Activity` view on its window's looper: every source's history,
the processes, the section shown, the Tune dialog (a window of its own
on the main window's looper, `open_window_here`, which has the main
window do what it sets). Each inspector is an `Inspector` view in a
window on a looper of its own (a tab of the app's window where the
session groups them), told each sample's account of its process
(`Seen`: the process, its parent's name, the machine's figures its
tabs go by), its details, and what every window knows (`Shared`: the
settings, the access, the sections this machine has, the supervisor's
state); it keeps its own CPU history. The hub passes on a sample only
from whoever measures now (the helper, with full access), so the
windows needn't know. What a window does to processes it does itself
(`act_all`, `quit_processes`: alerts are the asking window's), asking
the hub only for what's the app's: the helper's work with full access
(`Msg::Act`), asking for full access and doing what waited for it
(`Msg::GetAccess`), opening an inspector (`Msg::Inspect`), and an
inspector's menu commands that aren't about its process
(`Msg::Command`: the main window's, opened for it unless it only sets
something). Started for an inspector alone (`--inspect PID`) there is
no main window until it's asked for; closing the main window ends the
app, and closing the last inspector does when there's no main window.

`sections.rs` draws the cards from the kit's dashboard (`Card`s on the
gutter in a `ScrollView`, `legend`s, `Facts` in one or two columns,
`meter`s, small lists of processes drawn as facts are over a
`control_canvas` a row, which lights under the pointer and takes its
press; cards side by side flow in as many columns as fit, given the
room left of the scroll bar); its graphs are `Graph::live`, each
drawing itself again alone as its samples move a device pixel
(`Activity::graph_clock`: an interval behind the latest sample, so
lines scroll into the edge rather than jump); the Graphs section's
cards share the window's height evenly between their graphs. The view's
`body` runs once a sample; what it makes is compared with what the
window has, so a sample draws again only what changed. `processes.rs`
is a `ColumnListView` whose rows (`Rows`: each row's place, process and
name) are made only when the processes, the sort, the query, Tree or
what's folded change; its cells read the processes from the view as
they're drawn (a row is drawn again only when what it says does,
`row_key`), and a tree's triangles are drawn by the Name cell and
taken by `on_press` where they were drawn. The filters' menus are made
again only for a new list of processes. The search field is a view of
its own: its caret blinking draws nothing else. Settings are the main
window's while it's open; each change is told to the hub
(`Msg::Settings`), which writes them whole (beside, then renamed) on a
worker and tells the inspectors what's theirs (the graphs' span and
smoothness, the interval, the menus' checks); the main window writes
them at once as it closes and before an upgrade replaces the program.

On olo-kit against the GPUI build (release, 2× on a headless screen,
10 s each, under the same load): Overview 3.7% of a core (4.1: the UI
0.9 in both, on two threads now, the display's and the window's), the
same 11.9 frames a second at 472 µs each (598); Processes 5.1 (5.2),
its once-a-second frame 1.68 ms (1.67); 77.5 MB resident (77.9) and
78.9 (78.3); CPU 4.0 (4.8), 23.3 frames a second at 512 µs (22.5 at
920); Sensors, with its Fans card, 3.9 (3.8), 23.1 frames a second at
455 µs (11.4 at 686: two graphs the window's width there now, each
moving a device pixel at a time). The sampler thread is the same code,
and most of either.

Against the egui Activity Monitor (release, 2× on a headless screen,
each section 20 s, the UI thread alone; the sampler thread is the same
code): Overview 1.8% of a core (egui 2.0), CPU 3.9 (5.2), Memory 2.7
(3.5), Disks 2.6 (3.4), Network 2.8 (3.9), Sensors 3.4 (4.7), System
3.2 (3.5), Graphs 2.2 (2.9), Processes 0.7 (0.4: its once-a-second
frame is 6 ms to egui's 3.7); the same frames a second (a graph's
pixel at a time: 11 to 23); 93–96 MB resident (119–123).

`sample.rs` reads /proc and /sys on a worker: `probe` finds the sources
once (cores, frequencies, disks of a gigabyte and up, interfaces, the
GPU via Asahi's `agx_stats` or amdgpu's `gpu_busy_percent`, every hwmon
sensor named for people); each sample has a value per source (NaN until
a rate can be known) and a `System` of what isn't a series (policies,
zram, pressure, disks' requests, interfaces, battery, GPU, tunables,
volumes every 5 s, which skips network and FUSE file systems because
`statvfs` there can hang). Processes are read every sample (their
name, command and owner kept by pid and start time); connections and
GPU clients only while their sections show (`Control`). The network
comes from netlink (`olo_system::netdiag`, as `ss` and `ip -s link`
read it; the processes themselves from `olo_system::procs`, both moved
there for Deskbar's widgets' tips too): a
`sock_diag` dump of every TCP and UDP socket, v4 and v6, with TCP's
`tcp_info` (bytes acknowledged and received, at 120 and 128), and
`RTM_GETLINK`'s `IFLA_STATS64` for each interface's counters (with
/proc/net as the fallback). Each process's Sent and Received (columns
in the list, and the Network section's "Programs Using the Network")
are its TCP sockets' bytes since the last sample, a socket new since
counting in full; whose socket is whose comes from the processes'
`/proc/PID/fd` (`socket:[inode]`), read again only when a socket no one
is known to have moves bytes, or every 5 s while the connections list
shows. A process whose files can't be seen (another user's, without
full access) has none. Settings saved before those columns came in at
8 have their sort column moved along (`Settings::migrate`).

Sensors' Fans card (`sections::fans_card`, where there are fans to
read) is one graph of each fan's speed (to one scale; one that has
never turned left out beside ones that do), the processor's package
temperature (the hottest sensor where there's no package) and how
often a second the package was throttled for heat, each to its own
scale; under it the fan profile in use and the level Olo's fan service
holds with what asked for it, or why a chosen Cool isn't in force
(`sample::Cooling`, from `olo_system::fans::look`, the one reader of
the service's files; "The fans", below), and the throttling counted
(`cpu0/thermal_throttle/package_throttle_count` and its total time):
since the computer started, in the last minute and since the window
opened (`Activity::throttled_lately`), so a fan curve can be seen to
work. The sampler reads those few small files with each sample. It
had a reader of its own once, which took a missing status line for
"the fan service isn't running", of a service that was running and
hadn't changed the level yet.

A process's inspector (double-click, ⌘I, Inspect) reads `details.rs` on
a worker at each sample: General (program, command, folder, parent,
start, CPU time, scheduling, cores, context switches, I/O, control group,
namespaces it doesn't share, priority to change), Threads (CPU each, by
two readings), Open Files (sockets named as connections; double-click a
file for Tracker), Memory (smaps_rollup and mappings summed by file),
Environment, Resources (the cores it may run on, how the kernel
treats it when memory runs out, its limits: raise the soft limit to the
hard or lift both) and Supervisor (its findings, how sure and why,
whether it was lowered and why). Send Signal offers every common signal; Quit is
SIGTERM, Force Quit asks first. `actions.rs` does all of it (nice and
affinity for every thread; tunables only those in `TUNABLES`, governors
only those the CPU offers).

Processes chooses several the usual way (⇧-click a range, ⌘-click one
more, ⌘A all shown, ⇧ with the arrows): `Activity::selected` holds their
pids, following them as rows move, each leaving as its row leaves the
list (quit, filtered out), so an action never reaches a process not
shown chosen; in Tree a collapsed row stands for everything under it
(`chosen_pids`). The row menu, right-clicked on a chosen row, acts on
all of them ("Quit 3 Processes", Force Quit with one alert naming them:
"Force 3 processes to quit (sleep ×3)?", Send Signal, Priority checked
where all agree, Show Programs in Tracker each program once, Copy
Process IDs and Command Lines one a line), Inspect on the first; on a
row not chosen it chooses that one alone. The buttons under the list
and the Process menu act on the same set. Commands carry the pids
("quit:12,40,41", `pid_list`), so an agent's menu choice does the same;
refusals are said once (`act_all`), those wanting full access asked about
once.

Full access: `helper.rs` runs Activity Monitor's own program as root
(`olo-activity --helper`, through pkexec, which asks for the password
with Olo's polkit agent), and the sampler runs there, streaming samples,
details and actions' results back as JSON lines (NaN as null); the local
sampler pauses meanwhile. It asks at start (File ▸ Ask for Full Access
at Start, on by default), or when an action needs it (an alert offers
it, and does the action once it comes). It is only ever asked for in
the person's own session ("The person's own session", below; not on an
agent's screen): elsewhere polkit's dialog would come up on the
person's screen.
`OLO_ACTIVITY_HELPER=direct` runs the helper as this user, without
pkexec (tests: the whole protocol, nothing elevated); `=off` never.
**In tests, only ever signal, renice or limit a process you started,
found by its exact ID (`pid:N` in the search).**

`olo-activity --section NAME` opens at a section (`supervisor`,
`cpu`, …); `olo-activity --inspect PID` opens only that process's
inspector, at its Supervisor tab (the supervisor's alert and Deskbar's
gauge menu use it; with a copy running, both are handed to it).

## AirPlay (crates/airplay, `olo-airplay`)

Sending to an AirPlay receiver (Ben, 2026-11-12: a window, a
workspace, an agent screen or a video file, "high quality video and
audio"). docs/TODO.md has the plan and what a sender that isn't
Apple's may and may not do. So far: **finding the receivers**,
**pairing with one**, **playing a film on one**, **showing a window, a
display or an agent screen on one live**, with its sound, and **the
way to all of it from the desktop** (Preferences ▸ AirPlay, Show on
AirPlay and Play On in the menus, Deskbar's tray). A workspace that
isn't the one showing is still to come (app_server can capture a
display or a window, not yet a workspace).

- `olo_airplay::receivers(wait)` asks the networks the computer is on
  who offers `_airplay._tcp`, by mDNS, itself (`dns`: a question
  written, an answer's PTR, SRV, TXT, A and AAAA records read, names
  compressed or not; `browse`: asked from a port of its own with the
  answer wanted back to it alone, so no multicast group is joined and
  port 5353 isn't taken, beside Avahi or without it; asked at once,
  after 250 ms and after a second, the later times also for what an
  instance hasn't said yet). It blocks for `wait`: off a looper.
- `Receiver` is what one says of itself in its TXT record: its name,
  kind (an Apple TV, a Mac, a speaker, a television, by its model),
  where it is, AirPlay's feature bits and status flags, and what they
  mean here (`plays_video`, `shows_screens`, `plays_sound`,
  `asks_to_pair`).
- `olo-airplay list [--json] [--wait SECONDS]` prints them, for people
  and agents, with "paired" beside the ones paired with and "pairs
  first" beside the ones that ask. It prints and ends: no window.
- **Pairing** (`pairing`) is AirPlay 2's, which is HomeKit's. Once,
  with the code the receiver shows on its screen (`Setup::begin` asks
  it to show one, `finish(code, name)` proves the code both ways by
  SRP (`srp`: SRP-6a, the 3072-bit group, SHA-512) and swaps long-term
  Ed25519 keys under it): that leaves `Credentials`, each side's key
  for the other. Then at every connection `verify(credentials)` has
  each prove it holds its key (X25519, a signature each way) and gives
  a `Session`, whose `control()` is the `Cipher` the rest of that
  connection is spoken through (ChaCha20-Poly1305 in frames of up to
  1024 bytes) and whose `key(salt, info)` derives the others a play
  needs. `Http` is the connection (`request`, `encipher`); `Post` is
  what the pairing asks of one, so a test's receiver can stand behind
  it without a socket. The messages are TLV8 (`tlv8`). What an error
  is says what to tell the person (`Error`: the wrong code, asked to
  wait, refused, *not the receiver that was paired with*, forgotten by
  it, not reached).
- **What's kept** (`kept`): `airplay/pairings.json` in Olo's state
  folder, mode 0600 in a folder of mode 0700, written whole or not at
  all: each receiver's id, its name when paired with and its
  `Credentials` as one line (pyatv's form, so a pairing made with
  either reads in the other). A receiver is one by its id, whatever
  it's renamed to. A pairing's key lets its holder send to that
  receiver and nothing else; it could move into Passwords.
- `olo-airplay pair NAME [--code CODE] [--at HOST:PORT]` pairs (the
  code is asked for on the terminal when not given), `check NAME`
  proves a kept pairing at a new connection, `paired` lists them,
  `unpair NAME` forgets one here (the receiver keeps its side until
  the computer is removed there). NAME is a receiver's name or the
  start of it, in any case; `--at` says where it is without asking
  the network.
- **Playing a film** (`play`): the receiver is told where the film is
  and fetches and plays it itself, so the picture and sound are the
  file's own (nothing is decoded or encoded here, and a play costs
  this computer the file's reading). `Play::begin(at, credentials,
  what, options)` asks, and returns when the receiver has taken the
  request; `Play::next(seen, wait)` waits for how it goes on (`Now`:
  `Loading`, `Playing`, `Paused`, `Ended`, `Left`, `Failed` with why;
  where it is and how long it is); `pause(bool)`; dropping it stops
  the film there. It blocks while the receiver answers: off a looper.
  What it does, in order: connects and proves each side (`verify`),
  SETUP of the session, the *event channel* (`events`: a second
  connection the receiver speaks on, each thing answered or it closes
  the session within half a minute), RECORD, then asks for the film
  **the newer way** (what tvOS 26 and 27 take: SETUP of a stream of
  commands, then `POST /command` with `insertPlayQueueItem`,
  `setProperty` and `setRate`, and the receiver's `playbackState`
  events say how it goes) and, where a receiver doesn't take that,
  **the older way** (`POST /play`, then `GET /playback-info` asked
  every second). `/feedback` every two seconds keeps the session, as
  Apple's senders do; a receiver that asks the time is answered
  (`timing`). None of this is published: it follows pyatv (and the
  rework of its `play_url` for tvOS 26, its pull request 2846), and
  `Options::trace` (the command's `--trace`) says each step and what
  the receiver answered, for when a real one differs.
- **The film's file** (`serve`) is served to the receiver for the
  length of the play from a port on the address the receiver reaches
  this computer by: one file, whole or by Range (a receiver seeks by
  them), at a path of 128 random bits told only over the enciphered
  connection; anything else asked there is "not found"; gone when the
  play is. The file crosses the network in the clear, as every film
  played by its address does. What a receiver plays by itself is told
  by how the file begins (`play::kind_of`: MP4, QuickTime, MPEG-TS,
  MP3, AAC, WAV, AIFF, FLAC); Matroska, WebM, AVI and Ogg are refused
  with the reason, before anything is sent (converting on the way is
  the live path's work, not here yet).
- `olo-airplay play NAME FILE|ADDRESS [--from TIME] [--json] [--trace]`
  plays and says how it goes (a line when what it's doing changes;
  `--json`: a line of JSON each), ends when the film does, and stops
  it at the receiver on Ctrl-C or when told to end (the signals are
  waited for by a thread: nothing polls).
- **While a film plays**, its play is that process, and it says how it
  goes in a file of its own, `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-airplay/<pid>.json`
  (`olo_protocol::airplay::Playing`: the receiver, what plays, loading,
  playing or paused, where in the film it was and when that was, how
  long the film is). It's written when what the play is doing changes
  or where it is jumps, never as it goes (`position_now` reckons where
  it is by now), and gone when the play is; a file whose process isn't
  an `olo-airplay` any more counts for nothing (`alive`). A play is the
  session's, not a display's: the receiver is in the room, whoever
  asked. `olo-airplay playing [--json]` lists the plays;
  `olo-airplay stop|pause|resume [NAME] [--pid N]` tell them (every
  one, those on a receiver, or the one of that process), by a signal
  to the play's process (SIGTERM, SIGUSR1, SIGUSR2), which its signal
  thread acts on. **Deskbar's tray** follows the folder (inotify) and,
  while anything plays, has a screen with a play mark on it
  (`status::draw_airplay`: two bars while every play is paused, a
  count for more than one; the mark placed in device pixels inside the
  screen's frame, so it's centred at every scale), its tip and menu
  saying what plays where, with Pause (or Resume) and Stop for each
  and Stop All (`airplay:stop|pause|resume:PID`, which run the
  commands above). Measured with a film playing (release, a headless
  session): Deskbar 0.0% of a core and no frames, as with none; the
  play itself 0.0% of a core, one wakeup a second (its keep-alive).

**Showing a screen live** (`mirror`, `olo-airplay show`) is AirPlay's
mirroring as Apple's senders do it today, as doubletake (an LGPL
sender for Linux that works with today's Apple TVs) has found the
wire; written from what it says, none of its code. On a connection
proved by pair-verify everything is keyed from that connection's
secret, so there is **no FairPlay** (whose code is Apple's, or taken
from Apple's, and LGPL where it's open).

- `Mirror::begin(at, credentials, features, version, options)`: GET
  /info (the receiver's screen: `Screen`, its size and rate), SETUP of
  the session alone (the older form, the session with its sound, where
  that's refused), the event channel at once, a sound stream (type 96:
  ALAC, a key of ours in `shk`), a picture stream (110: H.264), RECORD,
  the volume. Time is told one of two ways (`clock`): NTP answers on
  our timing port, or, on receivers that keep a PTP clock of their own
  (feature 41, AirPlay 354.54.6 and later), stamps on that clock's
  timeline, laid against ours from each answer's
  `X-Apple-RequestReceivedTimestamp` (never moving back).
- Pictures (`video`) go on the data connection: a 128-byte header each,
  the decoder's configuration (avcC) plain when the parameter sets
  change, each access unit's slices length-prefixed and sealed with
  ChaCha20-Poly1305 (a key from the pairing's secret,
  `DataStream-Salt<id>`), stamped with its capture's moment plus a
  lead (`lead()`: 40 ms wired, 75 on Wi-Fi; `--lead MS`); a heartbeat
  a second. `show(annex_b, size, captured)` sends one.
- Sound (`sound`): 352-sample ALAC frames stored as they are (nothing
  to compress, nothing lost), RTP over UDP sealed with our key, its RTP
  time following the samples as they come (a slow average of how far
  the captured sound runs from the clock), a sync with the first
  packet and every second, packets the receiver missed sent again when
  asked (the last 512 kept). `sound(samples, captured)` sends them.
- `/feedback` every two seconds keeps it; it ends when the receiver
  closes the data connection or the event channel (`ended()`).
- `olo-airplay show RECEIVER [--window ID | --display NAME |
  --workspace N [--display NAME] | --screen AGENT-SCREEN] [--title
  TITLE] [--no-sound] [--fps N] [--encoder auto|vaapi|nvidia|cpu] [--lead MS]
  [--json] [--trace] [--notify]`: frames come from app_server's capture
  (`olo_capture`, as the recorder's do; a workspace, from 1, through
  Olo's workspace source, "Screen sharing" ▸ Workspaces, so it shows
  live though its display shows another), asked for at most at the rate the receiver takes and given only
  when something changed, so a still screen sends nothing but
  heartbeats. The newest waits for the encoder's worker (one that
  comes while the last is encoded takes its place, its buffer used
  again). Frames come the receiver's size (`Screen::fit`, its shape
  kept: a 2× display made smaller), drawn so by app_server on the GPU
  (a fitted source, `Capture::fit`, "Screen sharing" ▸ Fitted; from an
  older app_server, shrunk by the worker on the processor,
  `fast_image_resize`, the fourth byte not weighed as alpha); the
  worker encodes each (H.264, a picture out for each in, no B-frames:
  `encoder_for`, VA-API's on the GPU app_server draws on where its
  driver makes H.264, the Intel GPU's here, else NVENC at up to 60 a
  second where it opens, else OpenH264 at 30) and sends it. Frames for
  an encoder on the GPU that draws them are lent to it as they come
  (`Capture::lend_frames`, as the recorder's, "Frames that never leave
  the GPU": made NV12 by its video processor, never copied through the
  processor), when they are the receiver's size (fitted); the encoder
  tells the capture's thread which GPU it's on (`prime`), and one that
  refuses a lent frame sets that back to none, so the rest are copied.
  After a reload the new capture lends again. The sound plays on the
  receiver and not here, as macOS does it (`olo-airplay/sound.rs`): the
  showing makes an output of its own in process ("Den (AirPlay)", a
  PipeWire stream of class `Audio/Sink`, `olo-airplay.PID`, 44.1 kHz
  stereo, a cycle every 21 ms at most, `node.always-process` so the
  receiver's sound has no gaps, the lowest priority so nothing goes to
  it by itself) and moves to it the sound that goes with what's shown
  (`olo_system::audio::Streams`: the sound server's streams listed,
  followed as they come, moved by name): a window's, its app's streams
  (its process's and its children's, by `/proc`: a browser plays from
  a helper; app_server says the window's process); an agent screen's,
  its programs' (`OLO_SCREEN` in their environment); a display's or a
  workspace's, every stream on the default output (one the person sent
  elsewhere, a call on headphones, stays). The default output isn't
  changed (it's the person's, kept across logins). The volume keys set
  the receiver's own volume, as macOS's do: it is told the default
  output's volume when the showing starts and as it changes (AirPlay's
  `volume` parameter, the slider's place spread from -30 dB to 0, -144
  muted: `Mirror::set_volume`, told by the keeping-alive thread so the
  caller never waits), and the samples go at full scale, never made
  quieter here (which would lose their low bits). The TV's output made
  the default by the person has its own volume, which PipeWire applies;
  the receiver's then stays as it was. Paused, or
  ended, each stream goes back where it was: its output, or the
  default again for one that followed it (PipeWire then follows the
  default again). Killed, its output goes with the process and
  WirePlumber sends what was on it to the default: nothing is left
  playing nowhere. After a reload the window's process is asked again
  (`TvSound::follow`); when PipeWire goes, the output is made again.
  Where it can't be made (no PipeWire; a window whose process isn't
  known), the computer's sound as it plays here
  (`recording::Capture::start_as`, the default output's monitor),
  heard here and on the receiver. While paused, the receiver hears
  silence and keeps the last picture.
  SIGUSR1 pauses, SIGUSR2 goes on, SIGTERM stops, as for a play; it is
  said in the same folder (`Playing { live: true }`, "showing" or
  "paused"), so Deskbar's tray, `olo-airplay playing|pause|resume|stop`
  and agents see it as they see a play. It outlives app_server's
  reload or upgrade: a capture app_server ends is the showing's end
  only if the connection outlives it two seconds (what was shown went,
  a window closed); else it waits for app_server, trying every quarter
  second for half a minute, and captures again what `Capture::again`
  says (fitted again), the receiver keeping the last picture meanwhile.
  `--trace` also says each
  120 frames how long the resize, the encoding and capture-to-sent took.
- Measured (release, a headless 1920 × 1200 session at 2× shown on the
  test receiver, `tools/dev/cost`): a still screen 1.2% of a core
  (2.0% with the sound's 10 ms chunks), paused 1.2%; a Terminal
  printing nonstop, 57 frames a second of 1728 × 1080, 13.7% with
  frames fitted by app_server (32.4% shrinking them here: 3.3 ms a
  frame), NVENC 3.3 ms mostly waiting on the GPU, the capture's copy
  about 6%; 4.7 ms from capture to sent (6.6 at the 95th percentile).
  Frames lent to the Intel GPU's H.264 (RPM Fusion's iHD 26.3.5),
  measured against NVENC in the same session: olo-airplay 5.0% of a
  core (its encoder thread 4.4%, the capture's 0.6%) against 11.9%
  (6.6% and 5.3%: the copy out of the GPU), app_server 5.7% against
  5.6%, the NVIDIA GPU left asleep; 7.3 ms from capture to sent (7.5–9.0
  at the 95th percentile) against 4.7 (5.4–5.8): the video processor's
  conversion 1.7 ms and the encoding 5.6, well inside the 40 ms the
  receiver shows behind. 15.2 Mbit/s for the Terminal printing
  nonstop at 60 a second; a still screen 0.1% of a core, 7 wakeups a
  second (app_server 0.1%, 4). `--encoder nvidia` takes NVENC.
  The sound on its own output against the old monitor recording, a
  window of Viewer shown with a tone playing (a private PipeWire,
  `tools/dev/cost` on olo-airplay, pipewire and pipewire-pulse
  together): 2.3% of a core and 361 wakeups a second against 4.4% and
  1062; nothing playing, 0.7% and 97 against 3.0% and 853. (Asking
  for 10 ms cycles, as the monitor recording did, makes the whole
  graph run every 5.3 ms: 188 wakeups a second here alone.)

**From the desktop.** Preferences ▸ AirPlay (`apps/preferences/src/
airplay.rs`) lists the receivers that answer (asked when the panel
shows and by Search, on a thread, never on a timer) and those paired
with that didn't ("Not found"), each with its kind and how it is
(Paired, Not paired, Showing its code, Showing, Playing, Paused). Pair…
asks the receiver to show its code and opens a Pairing box whose field
has the keyboard: the code typed, Return (or Pair) pairs. A paired one
has Show Display (this computer's display on it, `Shown::Display`),
Check (pair-verify: "Den knows this computer.") and Forget; one
showing or playing has Stop. The pairings file and the plays' folder
are followed, so a pairing made by `olo-airplay pair` or a showing
started from a menu shows at once. Show on AirPlay and Play On are in
the menus (the kit's `Menu::airplay`, above), each running
`olo_protocol::airplay::show_on` or `play_on`
(`show_command`: `olo-airplay show --notify --on KEY --window ID
--title TITLE`, and the others; a workspace heading's menu in Deskbar
has Show on AirPlay ▸ for that workspace, `Shown::Workspace`, run as
`--workspace N --display NAME`); Deskbar's tray says a showing as it
says a play (its title, "on" the receiver, Pause, Stop) with AirPlay
Preferences… under them.

**Tests answer their own questions**: a responder of the test's own on
the loopback (`Via { to, from }` says where a question goes; `Via::lan`
is mDNS's group from every network), and a receiver of the test's own
to pair with (`pairing::fake::Receiver`, the other side of every
message, with a code, a memory of who paired and a `reset`;
`fake::serve` puts it on a loopback port, which `tests/cli.rs` runs
the built `olo-airplay` against by `--at`, its pairings in a state
folder of its own), and to play to (`play::fake::Tv`: it sets up the
session, asks the time, speaks on the event channel, fetches the film
from the address it's given, a part and then the whole, and "plays"
it for as long as the test says, in the newer way or only the older;
it can refuse, never come for the film, or leave; it keeps what it
was asked and what it fetched; a screen mirrored on it is opened with
the pairing's key and the sound with ours, and kept: `mirror::fake`).
To look at what shows while a film plays, `cargo run --release -p
olo-airplay --example fake-receiver [SECONDS [NAME…]]` is that
receiver run by hand (the loopback only; it prints where to pair with
it and where to play to it; `OLO_AIRPLAY_KEEP=DIR` writes each showing
it was sent as an MP4 and a WAV, with how many pictures and how far
apart), with `OLO_AIRPLAY_DIR` (where plays are said, in place of the
runtime folder's, which is the person's too), `XDG_STATE_HOME` (the
pairings) and `PULSE_SERVER` (`olo-fakesound`'s, whose monitor is a
660 Hz tone) set to the test's own. `tsession start` hands its
environment to the whole session, so a session started with them has
its Deskbar, its window menus and what they start keep to the test's
receivers and folders; `tsession run` gives a program only what's
said on its line. No
test asks the network it happens to be on, and nothing is ever sent to a real receiver by a test:
pairing with one and playing to one are the person's to do, at the
receiver. **So neither the pairing, the play nor the showing has yet
met a real receiver**: the pairing follows HomeKit's published
protocol and the paths and headers pyatv uses with Apple TVs, the play
follows pyatv's two ways, the showing doubletake's account of the
wire, and the first `olo-airplay pair` (or Preferences ▸ AirPlay's
Pair…), `olo-airplay play --trace` and `olo-airplay show --trace` at a
real screen are their real test (a receiver that
doesn't sign its key as HomeKit says is paired with all the same, and
said: `Paired::signed`).

## The fans (apps/fans, `olo-fans`)

A ThinkPad's fans run ahead of the heat, so the computer isn't slowed
down for it: the firmware's own curve waits for the processor to be
hot, falls behind, and the board's sensors pass the temperature at
which the firmware throttles the processor (their zones' passive trip,
65 °C on a P1). `olo-fans` is a root service (systemd's
`olo-fans.service`; the fans are root's to set, through
`/proc/acpi/ibm/fan` of thinkpad_acpi loaded with `fan_control=1`).
`/etc/olo/fans` holds the profile, one word: `auto` (the firmware's
own curve: nothing read or written, asleep until the file changes) or
`cool` (the firmware's curve while everything is cool, the fans raised
early as anything warms, up to full speed). There are only those two.
In `cool` it watches every sensor the computer has (each core and the
package, the firmware's own readings, every thermal zone with a trip,
the SSD, the memory), each with where the fans start for it and where
they're at full speed (`Sensor::span`, from its own limit), and sets
the level by the worst of three things: how near a sensor is to where
it would be throttled, how fast it's rising, and how much power the
processor draws (heat that hasn't reached a sensor yet). It comes down
a step at a time, after a hold. It is safe by the firmware's watchdog:
while it holds a level it says so every few seconds, and if it stops
the firmware takes the fans back within 30 seconds; ending, it hands
them back itself. `olo-fans --status` prints what it reads and would
do, changing nothing (as anyone); `/run/olo-fans/status` is a line of
`level=… why=…`, there from the service's start to its end and
written again when the level or the profile changes. Its source's doc
comment has the rest. Never run the service, or write a fan level,
from a test: `--status` and its unit tests only.

**It never ends for something it can't do**, and what it can't do is
said where people look. Two things went wrong on Ben's P1 on
2026-11-12, both from one cause: levels had been turned on by loading
thinkpad_acpi again by hand (`fan_control=1`), which that morning's
restart undid, and nothing kept the setting.

- The driver refuses every write then ("Invalid argument"). The
  service ended at its first, twice; systemd started it a third time
  into a cool moment, and it sat there, running, setting nothing and
  saying nothing (its status was written only when the level changed).
  Three ends in two minutes and systemd would have given it up for
  good. Now: where the driver doesn't take levels (`CONTROL`) nothing
  is tried; the fans are the firmware's; the service says so; it
  writes the file that turns levels on at the driver's next loading
  (`MODPROBE`: `olo_system::fans::CONF`, the same Olo Doctor's helper
  writes), and looks again once a minute, for a driver loaded again by
  hand. A level refused for any other reason is said once and tried
  again 30 seconds later (`Fans::refuse`).
- "Running" is the service's folder in /run (`Places::running`:
  systemd's `RuntimeDirectory`, there for the service's life and no
  longer), not its having said something. `State::amiss` is why a
  chosen Cool isn't in force (`Amiss`: the driver doesn't take levels
  and will from the next start; doesn't and nothing tells it to; the
  service isn't running), `State::level` the level held ("auto" for a
  running service that has said nothing), and `State::now` and
  Activity Monitor say those. A driver that doesn't take levels comes
  first: whatever the service says, nothing is set.

Olo Doctor finds each (`checks::fan_profile`, only where Cool is
chosen): "The Cool fan profile isn't in force" with Repair the Fan
Profile (the driver's file) or Start the Fan Service, "…starts with the
computer's next start" (nothing to fix), and "Olo's fan service runs
an older version" with Update the Fan Service, since root's copy is
one an upgrade doesn't replace. Its fix is `fans::steps`, the same
steps choosing Cool runs. Loading the driver again, which would put
levels in force without a restart, is not something Olo does (a
driver that didn't come back would take the Fn keys and the battery's
limits with it until the next start): by hand, as root,
`modprobe -r thinkpad_acpi && modprobe thinkpad_acpi`, then
`systemctl restart olo-fans`.

**Choosing the profile** (Ben, 2026-11-10: "have in the power prefs
the option for the default auto and this new cooler/louder auto
profile"). Three parts, each knowing only its own:

- `olo_system::fans` reads what there is, as anyone: whether the fans
  can be set at all (`look` is None without a ThinkPad's
  `/proc/acpi/ibm/fan`), the profile in force (`/etc/olo/fans`' while
  the service is installed, else the firmware's), whether
  thinkpad_acpi takes levels (`fan_control`), and the level the
  service holds and why (`State::now`: "Now: level 4 of 7, for 19 W.").
  It changes nothing.
- Olo Doctor sets it (`apps/doctor/src/fans.rs`), as it does the login
  screen's parts: `fans::steps(profile, bin, places)` are root steps
  for only what isn't so already. Cool: `olo-fans` copied from beside
  Doctor to `/usr/local/libexec/olo` (root's copy: an upgrade replaces
  the person's programs, not it, so choosing Cool again brings it up
  to date) with its SELinux label put right, its unit
  (`data/systemd/olo-fans.service`, carried in the program),
  `/etc/modprobe.d/olo-fans.conf` (`options thinkpad_acpi
  fan_control=1`), kept whether or not the driver takes levels now (it
  may only because someone loaded it again by hand) and, where it
  doesn't, in force from the computer's next start and said so, the
  word, and the unit
  enabled and, if its program or unit changed, started again (running
  already, the service reads the word by itself). Automatic: the word
  alone, and only where the service is installed. `olo-doctor --fans`
  says what there is; `olo-doctor --fans auto|cool` sets it, through
  the helper and pkexec (the password asked once), or there under
  sudo: the way in for a person at a terminal and for an agent. It is
  asked for only in the person's own session (`helper::run_as_root`
  goes by `helper::way`): from a test session or an agent's screen it
  says so and does nothing.
- Preferences ▸ Power ▸ Battery & Idle has the Fans box, only where
  `look` finds fans to set: "Fan profile:" (Automatic, Cool), what the
  chosen one means, and what the fans are doing now, read with the
  battery every five seconds while the panel is open. Choosing one
  runs `olo-doctor --fans WORD` on a thread ("Setting it: an
  administrator's password is asked…", the menu dimmed); refused or
  failed, the menu is back on the profile in force with why in red.
  It's in the settings index (`olo_xdg::settings`: "Fan profile").

`OLO_FANS_ROOT=DIR` puts every one of those places under DIR, for
tests: a made-up ThinkPad is two files (`proc/acpi/ibm/fan`,
`sys/module/thinkpad_acpi/parameters/fan_control` holding `Y`), Doctor
writes its steps there as the person with nothing of systemd's asked,
and a status written by hand (`run/olo-fans/status`) shows in the box.
The whole of it was driven so (2026-11-12): Cool chosen from the menu
(the program, unit and word written under DIR), the status following,
Automatic refused by a folder made read-only (said in red), the panel
reviewed at 1×, 1.25×, 1.5×, 1.75× and 2×, light and dark. On the
real computer it has not been chosen from the panel yet. Activity
Monitor's Fans card and Doctor's finding were looked at the same way
in each state (2026-11-12: a driver that takes no levels, kept and
not; the service stopped; running and silent; a level held; a level
refused), the card at 1×, 1.5× and 2×.

## The scheduler (`scx_lavd`, tools/build-scheduler.sh)

Which scheduler the computer runs under is the person's to choose
(Ben, 2026-11-10: "add to olo the ability to pick a custom scheduler in
preferences -> performance and the recommendation should be scx_lavd
and if the user enables it then olo should handle installing"): the
kernel's own (EEVDF), or LAVD, `scx_lavd` of sched-ext/scx (GPL-2.0;
the Latency-criticality Aware Virtual Deadline scheduler), loaded over
the kernel's through sched_ext (Linux 6.12 and later). LAVD is made
for a computer someone is sitting at: what is being waited for runs
first, long work around it. If it stops, or the kernel puts it out,
the kernel's own takes over again by itself.

It is built as the fans' profile is, in the same three parts:

- `olo_system::scheduler` reads what there is, as anyone: whether the
  kernel can load one at all (`look` is None without
  `/sys/kernel/sched_ext`), what starts with the computer (LAVD when
  its program and unit are installed and systemd's link to the unit
  is there, `multi-user.target.wants/olo-scheduler.service`), and what
  is loaded now, whoever loaded it (`state`, `root/ops`: "Now: LAVD
  1.1.4 is scheduling."; another's is named and said to be not Olo's;
  chosen but not loaded is said, with where to look).
- Olo Doctor sets it (`apps/doctor/src/scheduler.rs`):
  `olo-doctor --scheduler` says what there is, `olo-doctor
  --scheduler kernel|lavd` sets it, through the helper and pkexec, in
  the person's own session only. LAVD: the `olo-scx-lavd` beside
  Doctor copied to `/usr/local/libexec/olo/scx_lavd` (a root service
  must not run a file the person can write), its unit
  (`data/systemd/olo-scheduler.service`, carried in the program),
  enabled, and started (again, if either changed). With no
  `olo-scx-lavd` beside Doctor, root's copy serves if there is one;
  else it says LAVD isn't with this copy of Olo. The kernel's own:
  the unit disabled and stopped (LAVD unloads itself as it ends), its
  parts left for the next time.
- Preferences ▸ Performance has a Scheduler tab: the two as radio
  buttons, each with what it's for, what is scheduling now (read
  again every five seconds while the panel is open), and that it's
  the computer's, so choosing asks for an administrator's password
  ("Setting it…", the buttons dimmed; refused or failed, back on
  what's in force with why in red). Where the kernel can't load one
  the tab says so. `olo-preferences performance --tab Scheduler`
  opens it there.

**The program isn't Olo's and isn't in Olo's workspace.**
`tools/build-scheduler.sh` builds one named version (1.1.4) from its
published source (`cargo install --locked`, with the lock file it was
published with: it carries its own libbpf and vmlinux.h, and wants
clang and libelf's headers, which tools/setup.sh installs) and puts it
in `target/release` as `olo-scx-lavd`, so what carries Olo's programs
carries it: tools/install-session.sh and an upgrade from the Deskbar.
Nothing runs it from there. Two minutes the first time (1 min 47 s
here), and 4 GB while it builds (removed after); nothing when that
version is built already. Olo builds and runs without it. A release doesn't carry it
(`tools/release.sh` leaves it out): a GPL program is passed on with
its source, which is the publisher's to arrange (TODO).

`OLO_SCHEDULER_ROOT=DIR` puts every one of those places under DIR,
for tests: a made-up kernel is one file (`sys/kernel/sched_ext/state`
holding `disabled`), Doctor writes its steps there as the person (an
empty file stands for systemd's link), and `state` and `root/ops`
written by hand show in the panel. The whole of it was driven so
(2026-11-12): LAVD chosen from the panel (the built program, the unit
and the link under DIR), chosen-but-not-loaded said, then loaded,
the kernel's own again; the tab reviewed at 1×, 1.25×, 1.5×, 1.75×
and 2×, light and dark. **Never choose a scheduler on the real
computer from a test**: it is the whole machine's, and everything
running on it (the person's work, every measurement) changes with it.

## Olo Doctor (apps/doctor)

Looks the computer over for what gets in Olo's way and fixes it with a
button: each finding's own, or Fix All (one password for everything that
needs root). `checks.rs` finds; each `Finding` carries its `Fix` as
`Step`s (`fix.rs`: write a file, set a sysfs knob, remove a file, start,
stop, enable or disable a system unit through `olo_system::systemd`,
signal a process), all done in process. From a terminal or an agent:
`olo-doctor --report` (the findings as JSON), `olo-doctor --fix` (those
with a fix, by id), `olo-doctor --fix all|ID…` (what the buttons do: root
steps through the helper and pkexec, or, under sudo, run there with the
scan made for the sudo user), `olo-doctor --fans [auto|cool]` (the fan
profile: "The fans", above), `olo-doctor --scheduler [kernel|lavd]`
("The scheduler", above). What it looks for:

- **DiskBackup** (`diskbackup`, from its settings and its service's
  state file): not set up ("Nothing is backed up": said, no button,
  since where backups go is the person's to choose); its service not
  running (a problem: Start It); paused (Resume Backups); nothing whole
  for three days or three of its intervals (a problem, the last's reason
  said: Back Up Now); its key only in this computer's keyring (Keep Key
  in Passwords); else when it last backed up, as fine. Each fix is
  DiskBackup's own command line (`Step::StartProgram`: one of Olo's
  programs, `olo-…`, started as the person, never as root).
- **Input remappers** (keyd, xremap, Input Remapper, evremap, kmonad,
  Interception Tools): they grab the keyboards, and any mouse whose motion
  node has keys (a Logitech G309), and type through a virtual device, so
  Olo's key mapping and its per-mouse settings never reach them. Fixed by
  stopping and disabling the unit (or signalling a copy started by hand);
  one installed by hand under /usr/local is removed too (its /etc
  configuration is left).
- **Another desktop's daemons** in this session (GNOME Shell, Mutter,
  KWin, gsd-*): quit. Never another login's: a desktop shell of this user
  in another `session-N.scope` means that desktop is logged in there, and
  everything of it is its own.
- **GNOME's services Olo has its own in place of** (`GNOME_SERVICES`:
  dconf-service, GNOME's and GTK's portal backends, gvfs's daemons and
  volume monitors, GNOME Online Accounts, and GNOME Keyring while Olo's
  keyring answers), running in this session or as the user's services
  (not when GNOME is logged in elsewhere, nor an agent screen's:
  `OLO_SCREEN` in its environment, `on_a_screen`, its own session's,
  which starts its services again; the same for another desktop's
  daemons and old versions): advice, quit by the fix (what
  asks for dconf, a portal or the keyring reaches Olo's). None, and
  nothing of another desktop either: "Nothing of GNOME's runs".
- **USB input devices allowed to sleep** (an interface of class 03 with
  an input node under it, a receiver's paired devices a level down;
  `power/control` not `on`), and **Olo's udev rules** (95-olo-input,
  70-olo-displays; the Doctor carries them with `include_str!`) missing or
  out of date: installed and applied to what is plugged in now.
  The input rule is numbered to come *after* the smart-card readers'
  (`92_pcscd_ccid.rules`), and applies at every event of the device,
  not only as its interfaces come: that rule turns autosuspend on for
  anything with a smart-card interface when the device's driver
  binds, which the kernel says after the interfaces, so a YubiKey (a
  keyboard, a FIDO device and a smart card) was back to `auto` at
  every start and every plugging in, whatever Olo's rule (then
  71-olo-input) had set, and Doctor's fix lasted a day (`udevadm test
  --action=bind /sys/bus/usb/devices/PORT` shows which rule writes
  what, changing nothing). Where it was is taken away as the new one
  goes in.
- **A fix lasts.** What Doctor fixes stays fixed through a restart and
  a replugging, with nothing to press again (Ben, 2026-11-10, of a
  finding back after every reboot: "olo should just set ephemeral
  stuff like that as needed on startup"): a fix installs what makes
  the thing so (a rule, a unit, a file, a daemon told to remember),
  and writes today's value only beside that. `Step::WriteSysfs`
  alone is for nothing; it says so. Every fix was gone through
  (2026-11-12): three didn't last, the security key's (above), the
  Thunderbolt 5 ports' USB (below) and a Thunderbolt device let in
  (boltd is told to remember it, `Step::AllowThunderbolt`, where the
  kernel's `authorized` was written for the once).
- **rtkit** not running (the supervisor's priority tiers need it).
- **Bluetooth not listening for the AirPods** (only with AirPods
  paired): BlueZ started without its experimental interfaces, where its
  advertisement monitor is. Fixed by a drop-in
  (`/etc/systemd/system/bluetooth.service.d/olo.conf`, `--experimental`)
  and Bluetooth restarted.
- **A USB 2 device in a Thunderbolt 5 port may go unseen** (advice, where
  Intel's Barlow Ridge USB controller, 8086:5782, is present): Ben's
  YubiKey in such a port wasn't seen at all (2026-11-04; the kernel heard
  nothing) while USB 3 drives were and the key worked in another port.
  It says to use another port meanwhile, and Keep It Awake installs
  `75-olo-thunderbolt-usb.rules` (the controller's and its root hubs'
  `power/control` `on` at every start) and writes them now, so
  plugging the device in again tells whether the sleeping controller
  misses the plug; once awake, it's fine, and Let It Sleep (the way
  back) takes the rule away.
- **Voice processing's sound not realtime**: a voice service's PipeWire
  thread that rtkit refused (its processes-per-user limit reached).
  Fixed by an rtkit drop-in (`/etc/systemd/system/rtkit-daemon.service.d/olo.conf`:
  64 processes, 256 threads a user), systemd reloaded, rtkit restarted;
  then Doctor itself, as the person (rtkit gives only to a thread's own
  user), asks it again for those threads before it looks
  (`checks::after_fix`, a fix's after-step, off the UI thread). Left to
  the supervisor's retry a minute on, the look just after the fix still
  found them refused and the finding came back after "Fixed.".
- **Frames kept off the fast cores**: `kernel.sched_util_clamp_min`
  below 1024 caps the `uclamp.min` app_server's and the windows' threads
  ask for (rule 9): set to 1024, now and at boot (/etc/sysctl.d/
  80-olo-uclamp.conf); a kernel without `CONFIG_UCLAMP_TASK` is advice.
- **Olo programs on an old version** (their `exe` is a replaced file in
  ~/.local/bin; never the session, app_server or the proxies): quit. Not
  one finishing what it has before it goes (`finishing`: marked in
  `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-upgrade-waits`, the mark no older than the
  process, as olo-session leaves it): Quit Them stopped Token Pool's
  copy the session follows while it streamed its last answers after an
  upgrade, which left Token Pool running twice for two days (Ben,
  2026-11-07).
- **Token Pool running twice, or without its gateway** (`token_pool`:
  this session's olo-pool processes on the gateway's port, `OLO_POOL_PORT`
  or 17891, and which of them hold its listening socket, by
  `olo_system::listening`). A copy that serves nothing beside the one
  that serves ("Token Pool is running twice", its window showing no
  requests and taking the launches): Quit It (the session starts it
  again, and it keeps the one serving). None serving: "Token Pool's
  gateway isn't running", Start It Again (the same signal). Another
  program on the port: said, no button. Never the keeper
  (`OLO_POOL_KEEPER` in its environment), a copy finishing after handing
  over, a launch younger than 15 s, the command line's own (`--status`),
  nor one on a port of its own (a test's). Else which serves, as fine.
- **The login screen's entry** (/usr/share/wayland-sessions, or
  /usr/local/share's on an atomic system) missing or pointing at
  nothing.
- **Olo's own login screen** (`own_login_screen`, where Olo's build has
  olo-login and olo-greeter; not on an atomic Fedora, whose /etc and
  /usr/local Setup doesn't change; Ben, 2026-11-07: "the login screen
  should come up in olo doctor as something it can do for me"):
  another display manager's (`display-manager.service`'s link,
  `login_screen::display_manager`) is advice, "The login screen is
  GNOME's (GDM), not Olo's own", and Use Olo's Login Screen runs what
  the Installer's login-screen stage runs (`login_screen::steps`, the one
  list both use: programs copied to /usr/local/libexec/olo, data to
  /usr/local/share/olo, PAM, `pam_olo_keyring.so`, sysusers and
  tmpfiles, its user and folders, SELinux's labels, its unit, the other
  disabled and olo-login enabled), from the next start. Olo's already:
  fine, with Go Back to GDM (or SDDM) beside it as its undo
  (`login:own-undo`), unless a copy in libexec is older than the build
  in ~/.local/bin (an upgrade replaces those, not the copies:
  `login_screen::stale`), which is advice, Update the Login Screen
  (`login:own-older`).
- **Olo's Wi-Fi healer** (below) missing, out of date or stopped, on a
  machine whose Wi-Fi chip needs it (brcmfmac): installed as a root-owned
  copy, with its unit and NetworkManager's setting for the chip.
- **A second graphics card kept awake** (NVIDIA's, AMD's, not the one
  the computer started on; `power/control` "on", as it stays with no
  driver: nouveau failing on a new card): Let It Sleep installs
  `data/udev/72-olo-idle-gpu.rules` (runtime power management for such
  cards, at every start) and sets it now. On the ThinkPad P1 Gen 9 the
  RTX PRO 2000 went from D0 to D3cold.
- **A graphics card that stopped answering** (`gpu_stuck`: its
  `power/runtime_status` "error", the kernel's word for power
  management that failed, its driver not answering until it starts
  again: NVIDIA's after memory ran out on 2026-11-07, NVML saying "an
  internal driver error occurred"). NVIDIA's is started again without
  restarting the computer (Ben: "i don't want you to restart the
  machine just fix the card/driver or whatever"), Start It Again: the
  person's programs with its nodes open quit (`/dev/nvidia*`, its
  `/dev/dri` card and render node; named, each program once: Chrome
  writes its whole command line into its first word, so a process is
  named by its executable then), then one root step,
  `Step::RestartGpu`: the services that keep it open stopped
  (nvidia-powerd, nvidia-persistenced, Olo's own olo-gpu-follow, which
  holds NVML), its modules unloaded in order (nvidia_drm,
  nvidia_modeset, nvidia_uvm, nvidia_peermem, nvidia: `delete_module`
  with `O_NONBLOCK`, refused at once while anything has them open,
  asked again for 8 s, then the error names what has the nodes open),
  the card reset (`reset`: FLR, else its bus), taken off the bus and
  found again (`remove`, its bridge's `rescan`: a fresh device, its
  power management new), udev loading its driver by the card's PCI
  alias (nvidia_drm's) as at start, and the services started. Failing
  partway it leaves nothing off: the card's `uevent` told "add" (the
  driver loaded again) and the services started. Not while the
  session's display server has it open (a display on its ports): then
  what to do. Another maker's card stuck: said, a restart its fix.
- **A graphics card with no working driver** (NVIDIA's, no driver
  bound; nouveau loaded and gone says it tried): NVIDIA's driver
  (`akmod-nvidia`, built for each kernel) installed from the system's
  repositories when one has it (Fedora's NVIDIA repository, RPM
  Fusion's), else what to turn on; with Secure Boot, its key to enrol.
- **Intel graphics that can't decode H.264 and HEVC** (`intel_video`:
  an Intel GPU on Fedora, whose iHD leaves them out, and no full driver
  in `/usr/lib64/dri-nonfree` or `dri-freeworld`): RPM Fusion's
  `intel-media-driver` installed, its free and nonfree repositories
  added first where PackageKit doesn't find it (`Step::InstallRepository`:
  the release package downloaded from mirrors.rpmfusion.org, installed
  as a package file, the lists read again); on an atomic Fedora, what
  to do by hand. Fine once it's there ("Intel graphics decodes every
  video"). Olo's player decodes all four codecs there then
  (`olo_vaapi::decode`).
- **Built-in sound with no driver** (Intel's SOF bound, no sound card
  made of it: a new laptop's SoundWire codecs, named from
  `/sys/bus/soundwire/devices`): a newer kernel and firmware installed
  when PackageKit has updates for them (`DRIVER_PACKAGES`: the kernel,
  linux-firmware, alsa-sof, Cirrus and Intel audio firmware, GPU and
  Wi-Fi firmware), else said plainly that there isn't one yet.
- **Temporary files in memory** (`temp_files`, Ben 2026-11-05): /tmp a
  tmpfs (`olo_system::env::in_memory`, statfs) and the session's
  `TMPDIR` (systemd's user manager's, `env::manager_environment`, else
  Doctor's own) unset or in memory too. The fix (not root) writes
  `~/.config/environment.d/60-olo-tmpdir.conf` (`TMPDIR`, `TMP`, `TEMP` =
  /var/tmp; removing it undoes it), which the user manager reads at each
  login, and sets them in the running manager and D-Bus activation
  (`Step::SetSessionEnvironment`) for what starts from now on;
  olo-session takes them from that file as it starts, before any thread
  (`take_tmpdir`), so Deskbar's apps and Terminal's shells have them.
  Programs already running keep theirs until they start again.
- **The power button's helper** (`power_now`, on a computer with an
  ACPI power button, `Power Button` in /sys/class/input): Olo's
  `olo-power-now@.service` and its polkit rule (carried with
  `include_str!` from data/systemd and data/polkit) missing or out of
  date (advice: Install the Helper, Update the Helper): written, and
  systemd reloaded. It's what lets Preferences ▸ Keyboard ▸ Power
  Button's "immediately" restart or shut down at once.

Drivers and firmware come through PackageKit (`olo_system::packages`,
its D-Bus API: resolve, refresh, install, update, install a package
file; each a transaction waited on off the UI thread, its progress
followed): `Step::InstallPackages`, `Step::UpdatePackages` and
`Step::InstallRepository`, run as root by the helper, telling how they go (`Step::run_with`,
`FromHelper::Progress`) under the finding in the window ("Installing
akmod-nvidia: Downloading 42%") and on the command line. `Roots`'
`packages` and `updates` answer for the system's packages (tests: made
up).

Root is reached as Activity Monitor's is: the program run again through
pkexec (`olo-doctor --helper`, JSON lines of `ToHelper::Run { id, steps }`
and `FromHelper::Done`), asked for only in the person's own session;
`OLO_DOCTOR_HELPER=direct|off` as `OLO_ACTIVITY_HELPER`. After a fix the
report is taken again; what was fixed and is gone is listed under Fixed.
Scans run on a thread; nothing is polled: Check Again (⌘R), a fix, or
the app opened again looks again. What can't be found out says nothing,
never a problem: systemd's user manager busy past its 10 s (as it was
while memory ran low on 2026-11-07) left the watcher, started at login
before Doctor's TMPDIR fix, judging by its own environment, and the
tray said "Temporary files take memory" while the window said all was
well (Ben: "seems like some of the checks are flaky"). The session's
TMPDIR is the manager's, else what Olo's environment.d file sets, only
then Doctor's own (`session_tmpdir`); a unit systemd didn't say the
state of (the Wi-Fi healer's, rtkit's) is left until the next look.

`olo-doctor --report` prints the report as JSON (agents, scripts).
`olo-doctor --watch` is one of the real session's services
(`REAL_SHELL`, with no window: it is never a running app in Deskbar):
after 20 s it looks, and every 15 minutes after (Ben: "run periodically
like on startup and then maybe every 15 mins"; a look is a few hundred
milliseconds of a background thread), and a problem not told of before
(remembered in `~/.local/state/olo/doctor.json`; one fixed and back is
told again) is told in a notification whose click opens Olo Doctor;
then it follows the Wi-Fi healer's report by inotify and tells of each
reset and what came of it (`--notify` is the look alone). Every look
(the watcher's, the window's, the command line's: `checks::look`) writes
what it found that gets in the way or has a fix
(`olo_protocol::doctor::DoctorFound`, `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-doctor-found.json`);
Deskbar follows it by inotify and shows Olo Doctor's bag in the tray
while there is something, a click opening it. Tests build a
machine in a folder (`Roots { fs, bin, uid, scope, units }`) and check
the findings and their steps exactly.

Any finding can be ignored (Ben, 2026-11-07: "each item can be ignored
which puts it into an ignored section and also has a button for each
ignored item to still fix it if the user changes their mind but it
won't alert about ignored items or draw attention to them"): its
Ignore button, before its fix, keeps its id in
`~/.config/olo/doctor-ignored.json` (`ignored.rs`: `doctor` and
`suggestions`, by id), and every look sets those aside
(`checks::look`, `suggest::look`: `Report::set_aside` moves them from
`findings` to `ignored`), so the count, Fix All (Apply All), the tray's
bag, the watcher's notifications and `--fix all` leave them out. The
window lists them last, under Ignored: each title dim, with Stop
Ignoring and its own fix button, which fixes it as ever. From a
terminal or an agent: `olo-doctor --ignore ID…` and `--unignore ID…`
(`olo-suggestions` the same; with no ids, the ignored listed), and
`--report`'s `ignored`; `--fix` lists them as "ignored" and fixes one
only when it's named. A process list says each program once with its
processes ("GTK's portal backend (xdg-desktop-portal-gtk, processes
1625065 and 1625111)", `by_program`), and the title counts programs:
D-Bus had started GTK's portal backend six times, said six times over.

## Olo Suggestions (apps/doctor, `olo-suggestions`)

What Olo suggests for the best of it, none of it needed (Olo works the
same without): each with what it does and why, a button that applies it,
Apply All (⇧⌘A), and, once applied, a button that undoes it. It is Olo
Doctor's body (`apps/doctor` is a library with two programs: `app.rs`'s
window and command line by `Kind`), so a suggestion is a `Finding` whose
`Fix` is applied by the same steps and root helper, what's applied is a
`Fine` with an `Undo` beside it (`Report::undo`, found by
`Report::action` as a fix is), and `olo-suggestions --report` and
`--apply [all | ID…]` do from a terminal or an agent what the window
does (`all` never undoes). `suggest.rs` has them; `OLO_SUGGESTIONS_DEMO=
applied` shows them all applied, made up, to look at headless.

- **brush as the login shell**: brush (github.com/reubeno/brush), the
  bash-compatible shell in Rust, is built with Olo (`apps/brush`,
  `olo-brush`: `brush_shell::entry::run`, installed and upgraded with
  Olo's programs). Applied as root: Olo's build copied to
  /usr/local/bin/brush, listed in /etc/shells (`Step::AddShell`), tried
  (`Step::TryShell`: it runs `-c 'exit 0'`), and made the login shell
  through AccountsService (`Step::SetLoginShell`,
  `olo_system::accounts::set_shell`); the shell it was is kept first
  (`~/.config/olo/suggestions.json`) for the undo, else bash. A copy
  older than Olo's build is suggested again (Update brush). Terminal
  starts the account's shell as it is now (`pty::shell`: the password
  database first, `$SHELL` from login after), so its next window is
  brush at once.

- **olo-brush's process goes where the shell is**: brush keeps its
  working folder for what it runs, not as its own process's, so its
  `/proc/PID/cwd` stayed where it started, and Terminal (which reads a
  tab's folder there: its repository, worktree and PR, where a new tab
  opens) saw a tab `cd`'d into a worktree as still in its first folder.
  olo-brush's `prompt` hook (vendor/brush-interactive's, called as each
  prompt shows) moves the process there, as other shells move on `cd`.
- **Programs worth having** (`TOOLS`, `tool_list`): just, uv, mise and
  worktrunk (`wt`), each suggested while it's on no folder of PATH nor
  in ~/.local/bin or ~/.cargo/bin (where installers put them, which a
  session's PATH may not have), else said to be installed, and where.
  just and uv come from the system's repositories (`Step::InstallPackages`
  as root, PackageKit); mise and worktrunk, which Fedora doesn't carry,
  from their makers' latest GitHub release (`Step::InstallRelease`, as
  the person, to ~/.local/bin): `releases.rs` asks GitHub's API for the
  latest tag, downloads the asset (`{tag}` filled in: mise's bare
  `mise-{tag}-linux-x64`, worktrunk's `…-unknown-linux-musl.tar.xz`)
  and the SHA-256 its maker published (a SHASUMS256.txt, or the asset's
  own `.sha256`), refuses it if they differ, takes the program out of
  the archive (tar with liblzma or flate2) and puts it in place whole
  (written beside it as `.partial`, 0755, then renamed). Nothing is
  shelled out to; the download's share shows under the suggestion as it
  goes (`Msg::Progress`: a fix run as the person tells how it's going as
  the root helper's does). Olo doesn't take them away again. `cargo test
  -p olo-doctor installs_from_github -- --ignored` installs both, for
  real, into a scratch folder.
- **worktrunk's worktrees where Terminal makes them** (with `wt`
  there): its `worktree-path` in ~/.config/worktrunk/config.toml
  (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`'s if set) set to Terminal's place
  (`settings.terminal.worktrees`, asked of app_server) as worktrunk's
  template, `<place>/{{ repo }}/{{ branch | sanitize }}`: the folder
  Terminal's New Worktree… makes for any name it allows (no `/`, so
  `sanitize` changes nothing). Written with toml_edit, the rest of the
  file (comments too) as it was; the value it had is kept in
  suggestions.json for the undo (none: the key taken out again).

Each new suggestion is told once, ever, in a notification from Olo
Suggestions (`notify.rs`, run by the session's `olo-doctor --watch` at
each of its looks, after Olo Doctor's): "Olo has N suggestions" with
their titles, a click (or Show Suggestions) opening its window. What's
told is remembered by id and title (`Told::suggested` in
~/.local/state/olo/doctor.json, never forgotten, so one not taken isn't
told again, and Update brush after Use brush is), and one with nothing
to apply yet (brush before Olo's build of it) waits until it has. A look
costs under 10 ms (`olo-suggestions --apply` lists them: the whole
program, 0.00 s), four times an hour.

`--apply` with an id that isn't there (mistyped, or an option it
doesn't take) does nothing at all and exits 1, rather than applying the
ones it knows.
- **brush's suggestions from Olo's model (olo-complete)**: with
  Preferences ▸ Terminal ▸ Command Suggestions on
  (`~/.config/olo/complete.json` `enabled`, read by brush and the daemon
  with or without Olo's session), the grey hint after what's typed in
  brush is the model's.
  - `crates/complete` (`olo-complete`), the model and its arithmetic:
    `history` reads `.bash_history`/`.brush_history` (with `#<secs>`
    times) and Olo's record (`~/.local/state/olo/complete/
    history.jsonl`: each command with its folder, time and shell);
    `index` keeps per command its counts, folders, hours, weekdays,
    exit statuses, what follows what (one and two back) and each shell's
    last commands, offers the candidates that start with the line
    (at most 32) and gives each 16 features (`FEATURE_NAMES`). `kernels`
    is the model: 16 → 16 (ReLU) → a score, 289 numbers, a candidate's
    softmax over the line's candidates; scalar reference, NEON, AVX2+FMA
    (SSE2 without), each tested against the reference. (A GPU kernel was
    tried and dropped: 258 µs a suggestion through blade against 1 µs in
    NEON.) `Weights::baseline` is written by hand (the features weighed
    as they're meant). `train` replays the history as typing (examples
    at a few points in each command, from what was known before it) and
