  ("Last 10 Minutes") is chosen again every five seconds only while
  it's asked for. Loading 160,000 lines its worst frame is 3 ms
  (egui's 34), a live line one frame of under 1 ms to 3 (egui drew
  three a line), and it holds 17 MB less. Show in Context
  (⌘K, or a line's context menu) shows every line around one
  (`program:all level:debug since:all`), and Back returns to the search
  before. Show Only (a line's menu) sets `program:` to its program. The
  search's filters are kept from one run to the next, its words aren't
  (`search::filters_only`); settings from before (a menu each) become
  the text once.

For agents, the same query from the command line, reading the journal
directly: `olo-logs --print [--query TEXT] [--since
10m|2h|1d|today|boot|all] [--level debug|info|warning|error] [--program
NAME | --all-programs] [--find TEXT] [--json] [--follow]`, `--query` as
typed in the window's search and the others its filters (JSON lines:
time in UTC, program, pid, level, message). Tests: `cargo test -p olo-logs` (synthetic journal files
in both layouts); `-- --include-ignored` also reads this machine's
journal and highlights every line in it.

## Deskbar (apps/deskbar)

The Olo menu, the tray and the running applications, in the top-right
corner of every display (a layer surface each, namespace `deskbar`, no
keyboard: its menus take the keys as they open), on olo-kit. One
model (`Deskbar`: app_server's windows, workspaces and displays as
events say, the tray's status, other programs' tray items and launcher
badges) behind a lock (`Model`), kept by the app's looper (`Hub`:
what app_server, the status watchers and the tray say comes to it
through the app's proxy, `Msg`), that every display's bar (`BarView`,
on its window's own looper, which keeps only what the pointer is doing
over it) draws: a bar draws again when the hub says the model changed
(`BarMsg::Changed`; a bar that changes it, `Model::update`, has the
hub tell them all), the pointer moves onto something else in it (only
that bar), a dot shakes or drains, or the clock's minute (or second)
comes (a thread of its own, asleep between); idle, nothing runs. What
asks the person first (Restart and Shut Down, the upgrade) is the main
display's bar's to open (`Effect`), so there's one of each; Approve
Without Asking's window is the app's. The lock is held while a bar is
drawn: nothing a drawing calls may take it again (its closures do
later, as the pointer acts). Each bar is painted in one `canvas` (the egui drawing,
moved over: the tile and wordmark, the tray's well, headings, rows,
the lit workspace), with transparent hit areas over it for the pointer:
a left click as a click, the right and middle buttons as they're
pressed (menus open on the press, as BeOS's), hovering that lights and
a tip in a popup of its own (`olo_kit::tip`: the bar is narrower than
what its icons say). A tray icon opens its menu on either button (Ben,
2026-11-06), each menu ending with the app that tells more (Network's,
Displays', Power's, Sound's, Notifications' and Security's preferences,
Activity Monitor, Screenshot); one with no menu (Olo Doctor, the agent
screens, an upgrade) does what its click does on either; another
program's item shows its menu on either button, with "Open NAME" (its
activation) last, or is activated if it has none. The volume's wheel
still sets the volume; Mute is in its menu. The tray's glyphs (status.rs) are exact-coverage
paths and the GPU's discs, rings and arcs (`paint_sector`), straight
lines on device pixels. An application dragged out is a link to its
program (`olo_kit::dnd`, its icon and name under the pointer); files
dropped on one open with it, its row lit as they come over it. A
click on a running application's row with ⌘ held (Super on a Mac's
keys; Control too), or ⌘ held as an application is chosen in the Olo
menu (`run:` and `desktop:` items), starts it again as a process of its
own beside the one running (`launch_again`,
`DesktopEntry::launch_new_instance`): Olo's apps are started with
`OLO_NEW_INSTANCE=1` (`olo_xdg::NEW_INSTANCE`), for which the kit's
`instance::forward` hands nothing over (and clears it; `spawn_detached`
never passes it on), so the copy opens its own window and leaves the
launch socket to the first; another program does as it does (Chrome
opens a window in the one it has). Deskbar never has the keyboard, so
Wayland doesn't say what's held: it asks app_server at the click
(`Request::HeldModifiers`, the seat's keys as pressed). Tried headless:
⌘-clicking Terminal's row, and ⌘-choosing Terminal in Applications,
each started a second olo-terminal with its own window; plain, a
window in the one running. Bars
for displays that come are opened once the model's update is over (a
window draws as it opens, and its bar reads the model), before those
going are closed, so the app always has one. Approve Without Asking's
window (approve.rs) is the kit's alert frame with a `MenuField` and a
`ConversationField`. Release build, against the egui one: first frame
58–73 ms (egui 69–87), 57 MB resident (141), 30 pointer moves across it
32 frames, 0.8 ms each (egui drew 150). The tray's items are counted
before they're placed (one more than counted is drawn nowhere and
logged, never a crash: Olo Doctor's bag, uncounted, took Deskbar down
on its first start after an upgrade, 2026-11-04). The battery: a click
opens Preferences ▸ Power, a right-click the power mode (Performance,
Balanced, Power Saver, checked as the daemon says) and Power
Preferences…. Olo Doctor's bag shows while its last look found
something to fix (`olo_protocol::doctor::DoctorFound`, followed by
inotify); a click opens Olo Doctor. (A recording going wasn't counted
either, until 2026-11-07: the last item went undrawn while one was.)
DiskBackup's item shows once it's set up (and `in_deskbar`, the app's
Show in Deskbar): a drive in a circular arrow (`status::draw_backup`),
the arrow and the drive's light green while it backs up, tidies or
restores (green, not the selection's blue, so it shows with its menu
open), all dim while it isn't backing up (off, on battery, the service
not running), a red dot when the last didn't finish and an amber one
when nothing finished for three days (or three of its intervals). Its
status (`status::Backup`) holds only what the glyph and tip say, so the
state file's progress every 2 s while it runs draws nothing (measured:
5 frames in 20 s with a write every 2 s, 3 without, 0.0–0.1% of a
core); the menu reads the state as it opens: what it's doing, in
DiskBackup's own words (`Progress::lines`, `olo_protocol::diskbackup::
words`, the window's too; Ben, 2026-11-08: "it's also not entirely clear
to me what it means … what is read vs new and i'm backing up my whole
home dir which is hundreds of gigs so why doesn't it say anything about
that"): what it backs up (your home folder), how far through how much
and how long is left, files of files, what's new to the backup and
sent; counting what's there first; a stop finishing the pack it's
sending; a stop said calmly, with what it got through; deleting, how
many of how many; the last and the next, Back Up Now or Stop (Stop
Tidying, Validating, Deleting), Pause or Resume
Backups (`olo-diskbackup --now`, `--stop`, `--set enabled=…`), Restore
Files… (`olo-diskbackup --restore-window`) and DiskBackup…. The speaker's menu has None first
among the outputs (below). The tray's battery and links
follow UPower's display device and NetworkManager's signals
(`olo_system::battery::watch`, `network::watch_links`, each on a thread
that sleeps until one comes; the links on a bus connection of their own
that the bus sends only device state changes, NetworkManager's own (the
default route moving), and for each link connected its properties, its
addresses' and its access point's: a scanning adapter's access points
come and go several times a second here, and aren't asked for), so idle
it wakes 0 times a second (it was 7–9, polling every 4 s). A signal
that says only the access point's strength or the adapter's rate (what
comes every few seconds) is taken from the signal's own values
(`network::quick`); anything else reads the links again (about two dozen
calls, 3.5 ms here) and asks for the signals of what's connected again
only if that changed. Measured beside the old Wi-Fi-only watch over
60 s, idle on Ben's machine (Ethernet and Wi-Fi both up): under one
wakeup a second, against about two.

**AppImages** (`olo_appimage`, crates/appimage, shared with Tracker):
with a `~/AppImages` folder, the Olo menu has an AppImages item under
Applications, each AppImage in it by the name its own desktop entry
gives (else its file's, a version and machine trimmed:
"Obsidian-1.5.12.AppImage", Obsidian) with its own icon. A type 2
AppImage is an ELF runtime with a SquashFS image after its section
headers; that's read in process (`backhand`, no mounting), for the entry
and `.DirIcon` (followed through links), else the entry's `Icon=` by
name (at the top, or the largest in its hicolor theme). What was read is
kept in `~/.cache/olo/appimages` (the icon, PNG or SVG as given, named
by its bytes so copies share one, and `apps.json`, by path, size and
time, changed under an `flock` as Deskbar and Tracker both write it), so
each version of an AppImage is read once, by whichever app comes to it
first. The folder is followed (inotify, `olo_kit::watch`: made later,
removed, renamed back too), and a change lists it again on a worker, one
scan at a time with one more after it if it changed meanwhile (an
AppImage still downloading). Chosen, it runs; one not executable yet
(just downloaded) is made so first.

AppImages are themselves wherever an app shows (Ben, 2026-11-09: "if an
appimage has an icon in it for the app show that icon in the tracker,
when running in the deskbar apps, and anywhere else an icon is shown for
the app"). For each AppImage known, a desktop entry is kept in
`~/.cache/olo/appimages/applications`
(`olo_xdg::desktop_entry::appimages_dir`, the last of `app_dirs()`, so
an installed app of the same id wins): named by the AppImage's own
entry's id (`dbdelve.desktop`), `NoDisplay` (the Applications menu, the
palette and Open With leave it out: `~/AppImages` is listed on its own),
with `Exec` the AppImage (quoted for `sh -c`, its own `%f`/`%U` kept),
`Icon` the file taken out of it, its `StartupWMClass` and
`X-Olo-AppImage`. So every lookup of an app id (`find`, `find_among`,
`icon_for_app`) finds a running AppImage's name and icon as it finds an
installed app's: Deskbar's running apps, the Twitcher, the window
menu's Quit, notifications, the palette's windows. Of two with one id,
the one in `~/AppImages` is named, then the newest; an AppImage gone is
let go of (entry and icon) at the next change, and only entries that
changed are written. A window whose app id no entry gives is looked at
once by Deskbar, on a worker (`ask_processes`, each id once, not on
every window event): if its process is an AppImage's
(`olo_appimage::of_process`: the runtime's `APPIMAGE` and `APPDIR` in
`/proc/PID/environ`, and the program in that mount, so a program an
AppImage started isn't taken for it), that AppImage is read, and an id
its own entry doesn't give is kept for it (`learn`: another entry by that
name). The Twitcher, which looks each app up once, looks those no entry
gave up again as it's shown, on a worker, if an applications folder
changed since (`twitcher::recheck`, `desktop_entry::stamps`): an
AppImage's entry is made a moment after its first window. Tracker shows an AppImage's file (`.AppImage`, or an
extension-less program with the AppImage mark) with its icon
(`apps/tracker/src/appimages.rs`): asked for as an item is drawn,
read on a thread of its own (`olo_appimage::info`), the windows drawn
again only when an icon came; the kind's icon meanwhile. Third-party
PNG icons decode whatever their format (`olo_xdg::decode_png`
normalizes to 8 bits a channel: palettes, 16 bits, a transparent
colour): of the 3,980 PNG icons on Ben's machine (ours, /usr/share's,
the cache's), the 3,836 that decoded before are byte for byte the same,
and 144 more (palette ones, Adwaita's 16 px among them) now decode.
Tried in a tsession with a real AppImage (DBDelve) in `~/AppImages`,
in Downloads (with and without its extension) and in a folder nothing
looked at: Tracker showed each with its icon, and run from any of them
Deskbar listed it as DBDelve with its icon and the window menu said
"Quit DBDelve", at 1×, 1.25×, 1.5×, 1.75× and 2×, light and dark.

### Live widgets (widgets.rs, Preferences ▸ Deskbar)

Ben, 2026-11-07: "add a preferences app for the deskbar and in it
support configuring/adding live performance widgets into it e.g. cpu,
gpu, disk, network monitors etc. -- it should all be very customizable
in terms of where they appear on the deskbar, how they look, how often
they update, exactly what to show and so on". As BeOS's Pulse and
ProcessController put their bars in its tray.

* **Settings**: `Settings::deskbar` (`olo_protocol::deskbar`), kept by
  app_server, so Deskbar follows a change at once (`SettingsChanged`)
  and agents read and set them (`GetSettings`/`SetSettings`; a widget
  with only `id`, `measure` and `place` takes the rest as it comes).
  Each `Widget`: an `id`, what it measures (`Measure`: CPU, all or each
  core; memory, and swap; a GPU by PCI address; a disk's reads and
  writes; a volume's fullness; an interface's down and up; a hwmon
  temperature, "chip/label"; battery power), where (`Place`: an icon's
  place in the tray, a row under the tray, a row at the foot under the
  applications), its look (`Look`: graph, bars, heatmap, meter,
  number), its row's size, its name and value shown, how often it's
  read (`every_ms`, 250 ms to a minute), how far back its graph looks
  (`span_s`), its colour (a `Hue`, or the accent), and whether it's
  `beside` the one before it, sharing its row.
* **Readings**: `olo_system::meters` (Preferences' list of what there
  is too, `sources`: cores, GPUs, disks, volumes, interfaces, sensors,
  a battery): `/proc/stat`, `meminfo`, `diskstats`, `net/dev`, statvfs,
  hwmon, the battery's `power_now`, and the GPUs through
  `olo_system::gpu_load` (Activity Monitor's, moved there for both: a
  GPU asleep is never asked, an idle NVIDIA one only every 20 s, each
  question being use that keeps it awake, but every time for 8 s
  after it wakes, when what woke it is about to show). **A GPU is as
  busy as its busiest engine** (`gpu_load::busiest`): NVIDIA's
  graphics engine, encoder and decoder (`NvidiaNow::total`: its
  library counts NVENC and NVDEC apart from "GPU utilization", so a
  screen recording encoding on the card read as an idle GPU, and as
  one not worth asking; a 4K encode is graphics 14%, encoder 50%), and
  xe's render and media GTs' idle residencies. Activity Monitor has a
  series for each engine beside the card's own (`gpu-render`,
  `gpu-media`; `gpu1-render`, `gpu1-encode`, `gpu1-decode`), and a
  program's share of an NVIDIA card is the most of the three it
  uses. `cargo test -p olo-system watch_nvidia -- --ignored
  --nocapture` prints the card's engines a line a second, to run
  beside something that encodes on it (olo-video's
  `nvenc_cost_by_codec`); it never wakes a sleeping card. A worker (`deskbar-widgets`) reads each widget when
  it's due and sends them together (`Msg::Meters`); with no widgets
  there is no thread, and with the displays asleep or the screen locked
  nothing is read (`Live::pause`). What a widget draws is made once a
  reading (`Shown`: each series' levels over its history, rates against
  the highest in it, its value in words), not each frame.
* **Drawing**: tray widgets take the tray's first slots (a graph, bars,
  a heatmap or a meter in a sunken well, or the value in small
  figures); a row of its own has the name at the left and the value at
  the right (shortened, "↓27K ↑102K", or without the name, when both
  don't fit), the drawing between them in a small row and under them in
  a medium or large one. Widgets `beside` one another share a row
  (Ben: "more than 1 widget per row, e.g. a more compact representation
  of a combination of things", as iStat Menus' labels over little
  meters): equal cells `TIGHT` apart, each its name (shorter, "Mem",
  where the whole doesn't fit) over its drawing, its value beside the
  name only if it fits whole (a number's under it), the row as tall as
  its tallest. A tip says what it measures in full and each series'
  value; a click opens Activity Monitor; the other button, Activity
  Monitor and Deskbar Preferences…. Agents read each as a `Meter` with
  its value.
* **Motion** (Ben: "make the graphs etc in the deskbar widgets all
  animate smoothly like in activity monitor"; "even if e.g. something
  only updates once per second it still smoothly animates, including
  e.g heatmap the tiles should animate to the next state"): each
  reading is timed (`widgets::clock`), and a graph's right edge is an
  interval behind the latest (`graph_now`, Activity Monitor's `now`),
  so its line runs into the edge a device pixel at a time and stands
  still once readings stop; bars, meters and heatmap cells move from
  where they're drawn to each reading over the time between readings
  (a second at most), still at each end so one move runs into the next.
  Frames follow the pixels: a graph's when it has scrolled one, a
  level's when it has moved one (a heatmap's: a sixteenth of its
  colour), at most 60 a second, all on the window's one clock, none once
  nothing moves. They're drawn by a view of their own over the bar
  (`widgets::Layer`, a child of the bar's view): the bar lays them
  out (`Shelf`) and draws their ground, tips and clicks, the layer
  draws them; a reading or a step of motion draws the layer alone (the
  bar too only while a widget's tip is up, for its words).
* **Cost on olo-kit** against the GPUI build (release, 2× headless,
  the same five widgets: a tray's bars and number, two graphs and a
  meter, 20 s): 0.7% of a core (1.4), 78 wakeups a second (78), 12.8
  frames a second at 307 µs (15.8 at 494), 107.5 MB (107.9). With no
  widgets, on two displays at 1.5×: 0.0%, a frame each few seconds as
  the status watchers say something new (10 in 30 s, the GPUI build
  7), 452 µs each (570).
* **Cost** of the GPUI build, over 20 s on release builds at 2× (`tools/dev/cost`): no
  widgets, 0.1% of a core, 2 wakeups a second, 0.2 frames a second;
  eight (most read every second: three graphs, 16 cores' bars, a
  meter, a tray heatmap and number), 0.9%, 45 wakeups, 9.6 frames a
  second at 614 µs (a frame of the layer alone: ~200 µs of GPUI's own,
  ~27 µs a widget, ~200 submitting). Before they moved: 0.3%, 2.1
  frames a second at 773 µs, the whole bar each.
* **Tips' top five** (Ben: "for relevant widgets like cpu, gpu,
  memory, network make it so that hovering over the widget also shows
  the top 5 highest consuming processes"): with the pointer on a CPU,
  memory, GPU, network or disk widget, the worker looks at every
  process (`olo_system::procs::Sampler`, Activity Monitor's reading,
  ranked by `Rank`), twice 350 ms apart for a first rate, then every
  second, and the tip says them under its reading ("Using the most:",
  CPU as a share of the whole processor as the widget's, GPU as its
  share of that GPU, memory resident, network and disk a second), kept
  up to date as it shows (`tip::retext`, its reading too). No tip, no
  look, and the sampler (its memory of every process) goes as the
  pointer leaves. A look, 827 processes: 10 ms (disk counters only for
  a disk widget's, a second file each), 5 ms more for the sockets, and
  20 ms for who has each, at most every 3 s; the worker's share of a
  core while a tip shows: CPU 0.8%, network 1.2%, none after.
* **Backups** carry them with app_server's settings; from another
  computer, a widget measuring a GPU, disk, interface, sensor or volume
  this one hasn't measures its default instead, said
  (`backup::widgets_here`).

Preferences ▸ Deskbar (`deskbar.rs`) lists the widgets in order (Add
one of a kind after the chosen one, Remove, Move Up, Move Down) beside
the chosen one's settings (what it shows and which of it, where, look,
size, name and value, beside the one before it, how often, how far
back, colour), each changing the Deskbar at once; Defaults has none.

## The lock screen (crates/app_server/src/lock.rs, apps/lock)

`lock_screen()` (Ctrl+⌘Q, Deskbar ▸ Lock Screen, `Request::Lock`, the
display turning off for idleness when `power.lock_on_display_off`, logind
`PrepareForSleep` and `Lock`) covers every output in black at once, takes
keyboard focus away and starts `olo-lock` on a socket pair of its own
(WAYLAND_SOCKET): ext-session-lock is offered to that one client only. The
locker is restarted if it dies (at most every 2 s); the screen stays
black meanwhile, so the lock never fails open. While locked, input reaches
lock surfaces only, keybindings are off, and the displays sleep after a
minute. A marker, `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-locked-$WAYLAND_DISPLAY`
holding olo-session's pid, makes an app_server that reloaded or crashed
come back locked (only in the same session: display names get reused). Before sleep,
app_server holds a logind delay inhibitor until every output shows the lock
surface (or 3 s).

`olo-lock` (on olo-kit) uses `olo_kit::lock_session(app, build,
on_event)` (a window from `build` on every output, each on a looper of
its own, and on any added while locked; `on_event`, on the app's
looper, hears `Locked` once, `Outputs` when the windows covering
outputs changed, `Finished` if refused, each with those windows) and
`olo_kit::unlock_session()` (app_server has been told by the time it
returns; then quit). The lock itself (who is asked, what was answered)
is kept on the app's looper, apart from any window: each screen is told
what to show (`ScreenMsg::Shown`) and says what was typed through
`olo_kit::proxy()`; the first open window has the panel, and the next
one takes it if that window goes with its display. The Interface Kit
takes app_server's `WAYLAND_SOCKET` as a Wayland connection, and a lock
surface makes no commit before its first configure and checks the password with `olo_system::auth` (PAM via
libpam, on a thread) while listening for Touch ID with
`olo_system::fingerprint` and looking for the person's face
(`olo_system::face`). A security key doesn't unlock it (see "Security
keys": a key left plugged in mustn't open a computer someone found). Debug builds take `OLO_PAM_CONFDIR` +
`OLO_PAM_SERVICE` (passed through by tsession), so tests use a private
pam_exec service and never a real password; then (or with
`OLO_NO_FINGERPRINT=1`) it leaves the fingerprint reader alone, which is
the person's own:

```sh
printf 'auth required pam_exec.so expose_authtok quiet /path/check.sh\naccount required pam_permit.so\n' > $dir/exec
OLO_PAM_CONFDIR=$dir OLO_PAM_SERVICE=exec tools/dev/tsession start lk --light
tools/dev/tsession ipc lk '{"type":"lock"}'; tools/dev/tsession type lk secret; tools/dev/tsession key lk 28
```

## Olo Rescue (app_server rescue.rs, apps/rescue, `olo_protocol::rescue`)

Holding Ctrl+Shift+Super and pressing Delete (or Backspace, a Mac's
delete; either side's modifiers), from anywhere, whatever has the
keyboard, brings Olo Rescue: for when something has gone wrong and the
person can't see or can't drive the desktop. app_server reads the chord
on its input thread from the keys' physical codes, first of all
(`physical_key`: before the keymap and its profile, shortcuts other
programs took, keyboard hints, the overview, a layer surface that takes
every key), so no setting, remapping or program can hide it; the
Delete is seen by nobody, and Super let go after it is no tap (no
palette). It costs a key 1.4 ns, and checking whether Rescue is on (each
layer surface, each frame and pointer move) 0.32 ns
(`rescue::tests::rescue_cost`).

In Rescue:

* **Everything is put away.** Each display shows a workspace of its own,
  one past the person's (the count is one more meanwhile); only
  Rescue's own layer surfaces (namespace `olo-rescue`) are drawn,
  reached or given the keyboard (no Deskbar, desktop, banners or a
  layer that took every key), nor a full-screen window, nor the
  wallpaper. Shortcuts that would leave the workspace or open what it
  doesn't show are off (`rescue::in_rescue`: other workspaces, the
  overview, Show Desktop, hiding, the palette, hints, Find, a
  screenshot's selection); ⌘Tab switches among what's open in Rescue.
  Windows opened in Rescue (Preferences, say) open on it, over Rescue's
  surface (it's on the Bottom layer).
* **app_server runs on safe settings** (`rescue::safe`): each display on
  its own at its preferred mode and the largest of 2×, 1.5× and 1× that
  leaves it 1280×800 points (`safe_scale`: Olo's default 2× is too big
  for a 1080p monitor), unrotated, unmirrored, no VRR, HDR or Vivid;
  the built-in display the main one; night light off, no wallpaper, no
  screen saver; a screen at a quarter of its brightness or less
  brightened (and kept so); the keyboard's layout, variant, profile and
  terminal and browser apps kept (it types, and shortcuts are where the
  hands know them), its repeat, xkb options and hints, and the
  pointer's settings, as Olo comes.
* **The person's own settings are what clients see and change**:
  `GetSettings`, `SettingsChanged` and `Outputs` tell them (Outputs:
  each display's saved scale, rotation, mode, place, mirroring and
  colours, so Preferences ▸ Display shows what broke), and
  `SetSettings` and `ConfigureOutput` change them, saved at once, applied
  as Rescue ends (`AnvilState::told_settings`, `settings_changed`). So
  agents and tools reading `Outputs` in Rescue get the saved scale, not
  the safe one on screen (tsession's crops are then off).
* **olo-rescue** (apps/rescue) covers each display with a layer surface:
  on the main one, Rescue itself, on the others "Rescue is on …" and
  Show Rescue Here (only Rescue's takes the keyboard, and app_server
  gives it it as it shows). It asks rtkit for `RESCUE_NICE` (−15, over
  the compositor even) before it starts a thread, and depends on nothing
  of the session but app_server: a terminal of its own (term.rs:
  alacritty_terminal's emulator and PTY in process, `bash --noprofile
  --norc` so a broken profile or login shell can't take it; ⌃⇧C and
  ⌃⇧V, which the keymap makes ⌘C and ⌘V, as Rescue is a terminal to it;
  the wheel and ⇧Page Up/Down for the scrollback; selection by the
  pointer; deliberately apart from Terminal, no olo-termd or saved
  windows), the person's processes (busiest first, read on a thread
  every two seconds while it's up; End and Force End), Preferences'
  panels (`olo_xdg::apps::PREFERENCE_PANELS`; what's changed applies as
  Rescue ends), Reset Display Settings… (every display Olo's own again,
  brightness kept), Start Over (`olo-session reload`: Rescue stays on),
  Log Out… and Restart…, and Leave Rescue.

Pressed in Rescue, the keys bring olo-rescue back if it had gone. While
locked they change the displays (a lock screen must be seen to be
unlocked) and olo-rescue comes once the screen is unlocked: Rescue is
no way past the lock. Leaving (`Request::Rescue { on: false }`, Leave
Rescue) brings the person's settings back, each display's mode,
colours and VRR, and what was opened in Rescue onto the workspace its
display showed before. An app_server restarted in place in Rescue stays
in it, each display's workspace from before kept (handover.rs), and the
session starts app_server in Rescue (`OLO_RESCUE`) once it has crashed
twice in a minute, as a setting may be what it can't start with.

Agents: `{"type":"rescue","on":true}` and `false`, and `rescue` in
`PowerStatus` (and `PowerChanged`). `tools/dev/rescue-check` checks it
all in headless sessions: the keys (both sides, Delete and Backspace),
its shell taking the keyboard at once, each display's scale (2×, 1×,
1.5×) and the layout review on each, Leave Rescue clicked (the window
and the saved scale back), the keys while locked, and a restart in
place.

## DiskBackup (crates/diskbackup, `olo-diskbackup`)

Backups of the disk to the cloud (Google Drive first), continuous, in the
background, versioned, deduplicated, compressed and encrypted. Being built
in layers; done so far, **the engine** (crates/diskbackup):

- **Chunks** (`chunker.rs`): a file cut where its content says (FastCDC's
  gear hash, normalized: 256 KiB to 4 MiB, about 1 MiB), so bytes typed
  into the middle of a file change only the chunks around them (a test:
  30 bytes into 30 MB, at most two new chunks). A chunk's id is a keyed
  hash of what it holds (HMAC-SHA-256 under a key of the repository's:
  the same content anywhere is kept once, and ids say nothing without
  the key). Each is compressed (zstd 3, unless that saves under 3%) and
  sealed (XChaCha20-Poly1305, a random nonce each).
- **Packs** of about 128 MiB (`data/xx/<id>`; `PACK_TARGET`, Ben,
  2026-11-08: "the link is pretty fast i think 128mb is fine"): few large
  objects suit a slow store (a terabyte is about 8,000, listed by Drive
  1,000 a request); each ends with its own sealed list of what it holds,
  so the index can be made again from the packs. A pack is held whole in
  memory till it's sent: its room is reserved at once and kept for the
  next while a backup runs (`Repo::let_go` gives it back after), and the
  service keeps glibc's thresholds where 16 MiB packs had them (blocks
  under 16 MiB from the heap, its top trimmed past 32 MiB): else every
  chunk's buffers are pages mapped and zeroed afresh. Measured (a first
  backup of 313 MB to a folder): 0.92–1.02 s as with 16 MiB packs
  (0.98–0.99), 38.6k page faults (36k; 289k before the fixes), 164 MB at
  most while it runs (72), 33 MB once idle (47). Tests keep 16 MiB packs
  (`Repo::set_pack_sizes`) to have several. Trees go in packs of their
  own, of 16 MiB (`TREE_PACK_TARGET`: small, changing with every backup,
  fetched whole to read one), which the local cache keeps whole (still
  sealed): walking a snapshot
  (the next backup's unchanged files, browsing to restore, tidying) reads
  the disk, never a slow store. **The index** (`index/<id>`, sealed) says
  where each blob is; it's read at open (cached locally: index files never
  change) and again when it changed (`Repo::refresh`: new files added, all
  read again if any went). It goes up with each snapshot and every five
  minutes while packs do, so a backup stopped part way (or the computer
  turned off) loses at most a pack: the next goes on from there (a test:
  stopped once a pack had gone up, then 40 MiB backed up again from another
  `Repo`, at most 25 MiB sent).
- **Trees and snapshots** (`tree.rs`, `repo.rs`): a folder is a tree
  (name, kind, mode, modified and changed times, inode, size, a file's
  chunks, a folder's tree, a link's target), itself a blob, so an
  unchanged folder is the same blob. A snapshot (`snapshots/<id>`) is a
  moment's tree of `/` holding the folders backed up, every version
  whole, sharing what didn't change; with a summary (files, new and
  changed and unchanged, new bytes, stored bytes, time, errors).
- **Backing up** (`backup.rs`): a file whose size, times and inode are as
  in the last snapshot isn't read (its chunks taken as they were); the
  rest are read with O_NOATIME and let go of from the page cache after
  (`POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED`: the backup's reading isn't anyone's working
  set). Sockets, pipes and devices skipped; unreadable files said in the
  summary and left out; Stop at any point, and a failing store, stop the
  backup (never taken for a file that couldn't be read). **Unfinished
  backups** (Ben, 2026-11-08: "it needs to track in-progress / unfinished
  backups too and they need to resume if i start again and i need the
  ability to clean it up"): the walk keeps the folders under way as a
  stack of levels (each folder's node and what's been gone through in it),
  so what's done can be kept at any moment: every five minutes (between
  files) and when it's stopped, each level's nodes so far, the one under
  way below it last, become trees, and an *unfinished snapshot*
  (`unfinished/<id>`, `Repo::save_unfinished`) holds them, with the
  chunks of the file it was part way through (`Snapshot::extra`) and a
  summary so far; it replaces the one it kept before. It's no backup to
  restore from (`Repo::snapshots` doesn't list it). The next backup goes
  on from this computer's that got furthest: a file it holds as it is
  now is taken, not read (new or changed counted against the last
  finished one), and its new, sent and time add to the finished one's;
  once the walk is past where it stopped (a name after its last, on the
  way down to it), the older unfinished ones go, and once one finishes,
  all of them. A failure that isn't a stop keeps only the index of what
  went up (the last checkpoint goes on). Tested: stopped once a pack went
  up, an unfinished snapshot of part of a/, which tidying keeps whole;
  the next backup reads only the 12 − done files it hadn't got to, sends
  nothing again, and the unfinished one goes (`stopped_backup_kept_and_resumed`).
  Files are read
  into one 8 MiB buffer for the whole backup (one zeroed for each cost
  more than reading and keeping a small file did), and one zstd context
  compresses every chunk.
- **Excludes** (`exclude.rs`): groups of what can be made again (caches,
  Trash, Rust's target/ builds and Cargo's downloads, node_modules and
  frameworks' builds, Python's, Go's, Gradle's and Maven's, C/C++/Zig/
  Haskell/Elixir/Dart builds, containers and Flatpaks, editors' swap
  files; virtual machines' disks offered, off by default), the person's
  own patterns (`~/`, `**/`), and any folder with a `CACHEDIR.TAG`.
- **Restoring** (`restore.rs`): a file or folder of any snapshot put back
  anywhere, as it was (contents, permissions, modified times, links),
  each file written aside and renamed into place; `find` for browsing.
- **Stores** (`store.rs`): `Store` (put whole, get, get a range, list
  with sizes, delete); objects are written once under names of their
  content, so a slow or eventually consistent store never shows half of
  one. `LocalStore` (a folder) and `drive::Drive`.
- **Google Drive** (`drive.rs`): the repository's objects as files of
  one folder in My Drive ("Olo DiskBackup", found or made), named as the
  repository names them (a Drive name may hold a slash), through Drive's
  v3 API (ureq, rustls with the system's roots). Under 5 MiB in one
  multipart request; above, resumably in 8 MiB pieces, a piece that fails
  asked where it got to (`bytes */N`, its 308's Range) and gone on from
  there (no redirect followed: a 308 followed is lost). Google's 429, a
  rate limit's 403 and 5xx tried again up to 8 times, waiting 1 s to a
  minute, doubling, a little at random; a 401 fetches the token again.
  Every body paced by the speed limits as it's sent or read, 64 KiB at a
  time (`Paced`, with its length: never chunked). Each file's id kept
  from listings (a listing of a folder: `name contains 'index/'`, Drive's
  prefix match), found by name if need be. Tested against a Google of
  our own (`tests/support/google.rs`: a 429, a token run out, listings
  two a page, an upload's first piece cut part way): put, replace, get,
  ranges, list, delete, then a whole repository backed up (a 20 MiB file
  resumably), restored from another `Repo`, and tidied.
- **Signing in** (`oauth.rs`): each person's own OAuth client (a
  "Desktop app" in a Google Cloud project of theirs: `Client`, from its
  downloaded JSON or its ID and secret), Google's installed-app flow: the
  consent page in the browser, the answer to `http://127.0.0.1:PORT` (a
  port of its own each time), PKCE S256 and a state; the scopes
  `drive.file` (only the files DiskBackup makes: non-sensitive, so no
  review by Google) and `openid email` (whose Drive, said); the refresh
  token kept. An External app left in Testing is signed out after 7 days
  by Google: the setup has it published.
- **`config`**: the format and chunking, sealed: opening it is how a key
  is known to be the right one (`Error::WrongKey`). The key, 32 random
  bytes (`Key::to_hex`), is kept by Olo Passwords, not in the store.
- **Locks** (`lock.rs`, `locks/<random>`: host, process, time, sealed):
  backing up or restoring holds a shared one, tidying the only one
  (`Repo::lock`; `Error::Busy` says who's in the way). Taking one writes it
  first, then reads everyone else's, so of two that can't both be held
  each sees the other. A holder refreshes it every five minutes; one not
  refreshed for 30 minutes is stale (crashed, or a laptop asleep
  mid-backup), as is this computer's whose process is gone. A holder that
  went 20 minutes without refreshing (it slept) takes its lock as lost
  (`Error::LockLost`) and writes nothing more: what it wrote may have been
  tidied away meanwhile; the service opens the backup again and goes on.
- **Keeping** (`keep.rs`): every snapshot from the last hour (a backup a
  few minutes old isn't let go of when Back Up Now makes another), then
  the newest of each of the last so many hours, days, ISO weeks and
  months (local time; Settings' `keep`, 24/14/8/24 by default); each
  computer forgets only its own (another's are its to keep).
- **Tidying** (`prune.rs`): what every snapshot left uses (its trees,
  read once each from the cache, and their chunks); a pack nothing in it
  is used goes; one 30% unused, or one of eight or more small ones (a
  backup's last, partly filled), has what's used copied into new packs
  (sealed as it was: only checked whole) and goes; a blob kept twice kept
  once, in the pack most used. A pack no index names (a backup stopped
  before naming it, an index file lost) is read back from its own list
  first (`Repo::pack_header`: two small reads at its end) and taken into
  the index before the snapshots are walked, so what they use in it is
  kept and named again, and only one nothing uses goes (one whose list
  is damaged, too; one that couldn't be fetched stops the tidying
  instead): a lost index loses nothing. A backup whose parent's
  tree isn't in the index does the same first (`Repo::find_lost`), so
  what's unchanged isn't sent again. An index file that doesn't open or
  read (damaged in the store) is passed over wherever the index is read
  (`Repo::damaged_index_files`): the packs no index names are read back
  from their own lists at once, in memory, so the backup still opens,
  restores and dedups; the next backup names them in an index file of
  its own; and tidying, due within the hour then, lets go of the damaged
  file (`Pruned::index_files_damaged`). Only the index files naming a pack that goes
  are written again (and small ones, eight or more, put together), then
  they go, then the packs: stopped anywhere, nothing is lost. The cache's
  copies of what's gone go too.

  Unfinished snapshots count as snapshots here (and their `extra`
  chunks): what a stopped backup sent stays for the next. `unused` says
  what no snapshot uses (what a backup that stopped before keeping
  anything of its own left), from the cache's trees. `repair` is tidying
  with damaged packs (a check found them) copied from: what still opens
  whole in each is kept, a blob kept elsewhere too is kept from there
  (damaged packs are claimed last), and the pack goes; a pack missing is
  let go of from the index as any tidy does. The next backup then sends
  again what's lost, of the files still as they were, and an older backup
  needing the same chunks is whole again with them (by content).
- **Validating** (`verify.rs`, `check`; Ben, 2026-11-08: "backups also
  need to be validatable and should be validated at the end of each
  backup but i should be able to manually trigger a re-validate of any
  backup at any time"; "add a fast validate option which compares
  checksums and just spot-checks some samples … fast validate should be
  the default and the one that is done automatically after a backup.
  full validate is only when explicitly requested"): without restoring
  it, that everything a backup needs is in the store, whole. Fast (after
  each backup; Validate): its trees walked (from the cache), every blob
  they need found in the index, every pack holding them listed in the
  store and as long as it was written, and the tree packs fetched from the
  store itself (not the cache) and checked against their ids (a keyed hash
  of the whole pack: exactly as written), each tree in them opened (a pack
  checked whole before is kept in the cache's `checked` list and not
  fetched again); where the store keeps a checksum of each object
  (`Store::keeps_checksums`, `Store::checksums`: Google Drive's
  `md5Checksum`, listed with the files), each pack's compared with the MD5
  summed as it was sent (`Repo::finish_pack`, in the cache's `sums`; or as
  it was last read back whole): it arrived and stayed as sent, nothing
  fetched; one that differs is fetched and checked; and a few data packs
  read back whole as samples (one in a hundred, one to four: those never
  read back first, so over time they go round all of them). Full
  (Validate Fully): every pack it uses fetched and checked so, whatever
  was checked before, and each blob of its opened and checked against its
  own id, as a restore would.
  `Checked` says what's wrong plainly (missing, cut short, damaged, lists
  unreadable), the first twelve files (or folders) that can't come back as
  they were and how many, the packs shown sent by checksum and sampled,
  and the bad packs, for `repair`. Tested: whole after a backup, fast and
  fully (every byte read back); in a folder (no checksums), a data pack
  damaged found fully (fast, only if it's the sample), one gone found
  either way; after `repair` and another backup, both backups whole and
  the first restores (`checked_damaged_repaired`); on Google Drive (our
  own), fast: every pack shown as sent by its checksum and one sample read
  back, then a pack changed in Drive found by its checksum, fetched, and
  found damaged (`tests/drive.rs`).
- **Speed limits** (`store::Limit`; Ben: "make sure that i can also set
  a max upload/download speed"): bytes a second each way, 0 for none,
  changed live; a store paces its transfers a 256 KiB piece at a time
  (`Throttled` for one that doesn't pace itself), up to a quarter second's
  worth at once, so the network never sees a burst at full speed. It
  counts what it lets through (`Limit::passed`): what's sent, live, and a
  pack's progress while a stop waits for it (`Repo::sending`).

**The service** (apps/diskbackup, `olo-diskbackup --service`; olo-session
runs it in the logged-in session): every thread at the priority chosen
(`Settings::priority`, This Computer ▸ Back up): Idle (SCHED_IDLE and
the idle I/O class: anything else that wants them goes first; the
default), Low (SCHED_BATCH, nice 19, best-effort I/O 7) or Normal
(SCHED_OTHER, nice 0, best-effort 4); a change follows at once when it
lowers it, and when it raises it (the session's `RLIMIT_NICE` is 0: an
unprivileged process can't) the service ends with 0, to be started again
by olo-session at the session's own priority and lowered from there.
Asleep until a backup is due (`every_minutes` after the last; never, if
`automatic` is off: Back Up Now only, and Doctor says so only after a
week), its settings change (inotify) or it's asked on its socket
(`olo_protocol::diskbackup::Request`: Back Up Now, Stop, Tidy,
Snapshots, Delete, Erase All). `Snapshots` lists this backup's snapshots
(`SnapshotInfo`: when, files, size, new and changed, stored, how long),
`Delete { snapshots }` forgets those (the exclusive lock) and tidies at
once (`Doing::Deleting { what }`, said the moment it's asked: opening the
backup, its lists, then the tidy's steps), `EraseAll` deletes everything
the store holds (its config last: stopped half way, it's still a backup)
and makes a new one there with the same key (`Doing::Erasing`, its
progress files of all); on Google Drive it deletes the backups' folder
whole, in one request however many files (`Drive::delete_folder`; Ben:
"can we just have it delete the olo backup folder in gdrive then
re-create it"), and makes it again, the settings following the new
folder; another computer finds it by its name when its own is gone
(`target::drive_folder_moved`, from `opened`). 6.7 s on our own Google
at 400 ms a request, opening and all. Tidying says its step (1 to 5:
what's kept, what the backups use, copying what's still used out of
packs mostly unused, the index, deleting what isn't used), with how many
of how many, and while deleting, what's freed of how much; it deletes 8
at a time (`DELETERS`), each still under the only lock, Stop looked for
before each (5.8 s → 3.8 s for 6 packs at 400 ms a request, the rest
being listings; the more packs, the more it saves). The state is written
every 2 s while something runs, and at once (within a quarter second)
when its stage or tidying's step changes or Stop is asked. A backup's
plan: the last snapshot's totals ("about", `Progress::estimated`), or,
for the first, a count of what there is first (`backup::count`, the
same walk without reading: `Stage::Counting`); then `Stage::Reading`
(bytes and files against those totals, the file it's at, `uploaded`:
what it has sent) and `Stage::Saving` (its trees and the snapshot). A
backup the person stopped says `STOPPED` (`Last::stopped`): said calmly,
never as trouble (DiskBackup, Deskbar, Doctor). What one that didn't
finish got through is `State::unfinished` (`Unfinished`: when, files and
bytes done, new, what it sent, time): this computer's unfinished
snapshot that got furthest, or, found once when the service starts after
one that stopped (since the last tidy) with nothing kept of its own,
what no snapshot uses (`unused`: sent, in no snapshot). A resumed
backup's progress says `resuming`; `Delete { unfinished: true }` forgets
this computer's unfinished snapshots and tidies, freeing what they sent.
Each backup is validated fast once it's made (`Stage::Checking`, `check`
with the shared lock still held): the result is `Last::check` (Validate's
of the newest too) and the snapshot's `SnapshotInfo::check`;
`Request::Validate { snapshots, full }` validates chosen ones, fast or
fully (`Doing::Validating`, its progress bytes read back of the packs'
total, the pack it's at), one after another, each one's `Check` (`full`,
`by_checksum`, `sampled`) kept by snapshot id across restarts (the state
folder, forgotten with the snapshot). Stopped, a backup says
`Stage::Stopping` at once (the service's state, from the stop itself:
the backup sees it only once the pack it's sending has gone), with that
pack's progress (`Progress::sending`, `sending_done`, and how long at the
upload limit), then what's done is kept: up to a pack's worth to wait
(at 2 MB/s, about a minute; the window says so the moment Stop is
clicked, and Stop is off). **Upgrades** (Ben: "make sure that upgrades
will work properly when a backup is underway it should seamlessly still
move over to the new process and resume there"): olo-session's SIGURG
(`olo_kit_base::restore::on_upgrade`) stops what's under way the way
that keeps its place (erasing is let finish), marks the service as
finishing something (`mark_waiting`, so olo-session doesn't stop it at
90 s), notes what to go on with (`Kept::resume`: the backup, the tidy,
the backups being validated, and what was asked and not done), and the
loop becomes the new version in the same process
(`exec_new_version`), which goes straight on: "Resuming the backup", no
stop said. Checked: the binary replaced as an install does it, mid
backup at 2 MB/s, Stopping within half a second, the pack it was sending
15 → 127 of 134 MB in 55 s, then the same process as the new version,
resuming; idle, at once. The bad packs a check finds are kept too, and the
tidy right after repairs them (`repair`; a tidy that can't take the lock
leaves them for the next). Doctor says when the last backup checked
isn't whole (`diskbackup:damaged`, Back Up Now). With nowhere to back up
(disconnected), the backup isn't kept open (nor Tracker's lookups). Waits
for power on battery unless allowed (`on_battery`), looking again every
five minutes then. A backup holds a shared lock, reads the index again if
another computer changed it, and takes unchanged files from the last snapshot
of this computer's (its host name), leaves out the exclude groups chosen,
the person's patterns, its own cache and a folder target; its progress in
the state file (`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-diskbackup.json`, `State`) every 2 s
while it runs and not otherwise; the last's outcome kept across restarts
(the state folder). After it, this computer's snapshots past keeping are
forgotten; once a day (an hour, if the last didn't finish), or when asked,
the backup is tidied with the only lock (another computer using it: next
time), `Doing::Pruning` in the state, then `State::tidied` (snapshots let
go of since, bytes freed) and `State::size` (what the backups take there,
grown by each backup since). A failed backup or tidy opens the backup
again next time. One service at a time: another started while one runs
(Doctor's Start It, by hand) says so and exits. Settings: `~/.config/olo/diskbackup.json`
(`olo_protocol::diskbackup::Settings`: target, paths, exclude groups and
patterns, every, keep, speed limits, battery, one file system). The key:
in the login keyring (`olo_system::secrets::DISKBACKUP_KEY`, which the
settings backup carries too), where the service finds it with no one
there; Passwords keeps it as well (the app, next). Command line:
`--status [--json]`, `--now`, `--stop`, `--set-up-folder PATH`,
`--keep-key` (the key kept in Passwords, as Keep Key in Passwords does:
Olo Doctor's fix), `--snapshots`, `--restore SNAPSHOT PATH [TO]` (a shared lock, waiting
for a tidy under way), `--tidy` (asked of the service if it runs, else
done there), `--set KEY=VALUE…` (enabled, battery, every, upload,
download, paths, exclude, groups, hourly, daily, weekly, monthly),
`--groups`, `--delete SNAPSHOT…` (an id's start is enough; `unfinished`
the one that didn't finish), `--validate [--full] SNAPSHOT…` (`latest`,
`all`),
`--erase-all --yes`, `--set automatic=on|off`, `--set
priority=idle|low|normal`; `--snapshots` says how each was last checked,
and lists the unfinished ones. For
tests, `OLO_DISKBACKUP_DIR` keeps its settings, state and
socket apart and `OLO_DISKBACKUP_KEY` gives the key. Checked so (a
sandbox HOME, a folder target): set up, the first backup at once (9
files, node_modules left out), a change and Back Up Now (1 changed,
nothing new), the older version restored, 5 MB new at a 500 KB/s upload
limit in 10.06 s; its scheduling policy 5 (SCHED_IDLE).

**The app** (`olo-diskbackup` with no arguments; `app.rs`, its window
in `window.rs`; Ben, 2026-11-08: "improve the ux in diskbackup … it's
complicated and not intuitive"; "where are the settings for limiting
up/down speed and resource usage and knowing exactly what's being backed
up now what the plan is what's still remaining"; "i should also be able
to choose if i even want auto backups … clear out / remove old backups to
start fresh"). Not set up, it asks one question, where backups go (A Disk
or Folder, Google Drive: side by side), and says what happens then. Set
up, a header says whether your files are safe (`headline`: "Backed up
12 minutes ago", "Backup stopped", "The backup … didn't finish" in red,
where to and when next, the last one's figures) beside Restore… and Back
Up Now (Stop while it runs); while a backup runs, the file it's at is
the header's second line (`StringView::cut`) and the whole width under
it the plan: "Backing up your home folder" (what), a bar of what's gone
through against the plan's (by the last backup's: "of about", and past
it "more than the last backup's"), files of files, time left (once 2%
and ten seconds are done), then what's new to the backup and what's sent,
compressed and encrypted, how fast, against the upload limit (Ben: "what
is read vs new"); each folder's turn (✓ ▸ ○) when there are several;
stopping, the pack it's finishing sending, of how much, and how long;
tidying and deleting, the step, how many of how many and what's freed;
erasing, a bar of what's deleted; checking after a backup, and validating, a bar
of what's read back and the pack it's at. "Resuming the backup" when it
goes on from an unfinished one. Idle, a dim line under the last one's
figures says what an unfinished backup got through and that the next
goes on from there (`unfinished_words`), and "Checked: all there." ends
the figures once the backup was checked. A slim reminder when the key is
only on this computer (Keep Key in Passwords), and one when the last
backup checked isn't whole (what's wrong; Back Up Now). Then five tabs: **Schedule** (When to
Back Up: Automatically, every 15 minutes to a day, or Only when I click
Back Up Now; on battery or not; Backups Kept: one an hour, a day, a week,
a month, for how long, said plainly as a sentence, `keep_words`),
**Files** (the folders, added and removed, and what the last backup
held; Leave Out: each group a check box named for what it leaves out,
its folders in its tip, and the person's own patterns, how they go in
the field's tip), **Backups** (the unfinished one first, "Unfinished
(14:05)", then every snapshot: When, Files, Size, New, Took, Validated:
✓ Fast, ✓ Full, ✗ Damaged, Not checked or —; a line under the list says
the one chosen in full, `check_words`, cut to a line with all of it in its tip:
when and how it was validated, what's wrong and which files; Restore…
opens the Restore window; Validate validates those chosen fast, at
once; Validate Fully… reads every byte back, asked first; those
chosen, one or several, the unfinished one too, deleted with Delete N
Backups…, asked first, saying what deleting the unfinished one frees;
Erase All Backups…, asked first, saying whether a fresh one starts at
once),
**Speed & Resources** (Network: upload and download limits; This
Computer: the priority, each level explained) and **Destination** (what
it's connected to, looked at each time the tab is chosen, on a worker,
`target::look_at`: Google Drive's account and folder, "Connected", what
the backups take there and the Drive's space, as Google's `about` says,
or why it isn't connected, with Sign In Again…; a folder's name, path and
its disk's space, `statvfs`, or that it isn't there; Disconnect… (Ben,
2026-11-08: "when i'm connected it should show the details of that
connection and a button to disconnect it if i want and then it shows the
button to connect again": asked first; what's under way stopped, the
sign-in forgotten on this computer, its refresh token gone from the
keyring and the client kept, `target::forget_google`, not revoked at
Google, which would sign out every computer using that client; the
target none, so the window asks where backups go again, Connect Google
Drive…, whose setup window fills in the client from before,
`target::known_client`, with the steps to make one folded away, Show the
Steps to see them), Use a Folder Instead… or Choose Another
Folder… and Use Google Drive Instead…, Open in Google Drive or Show in
Tracker; the key; Show DiskBackup in Deskbar). The window follows the chosen tab's height
(`WindowOptions::fixed`): every tab fits 1280 × 800 while a backup runs
(712 points at most, measured). Every change is written to the settings,
which the service follows at once, and is a step for Edit ▸ Undo. Live
from the state file (inotify: nothing ticks while nothing happens); the
snapshots asked again when a backup, delete or erase ends. Keep Key in
Passwords: the keychain's `KeepSecret`, a Password item "DiskBackup Key"
with a note saying what it is, synced to 1Password like any; Passwords
started if it isn't running, unlocked if it asks. The keychain's
`Secrets` reads an Olo program's secrets back by title (another
computer's setup, next).

**Tracker's ticks and versions**: the service answers on its socket from
a reader of this computer's snapshots' trees (`Repo::tree_reader`: where
each tree is, read from the cache's tree packs, the last 512 kept),
made again after it opens the backup (at start, not only at the first
backup), after each backup and after each tidy, so it never waits for
one to finish: `Request::Marks { dir }` (which of the folder's files
the newest snapshot holds as they are now: `backup::unchanged_since`,
by size, times and inode; 0.08 ms here), `Request::Versions { path }`
(`restore::versions`: one for each content the file had, newest first,
the newest and oldest snapshot keeping it, whether it's what's there
now; 0.06 ms). `--marks DIR` and `--versions PATH` ask them from the
command line. The **Versions window** (`versions.rs`;
`--versions-window PATH`, Tracker's Older Versions…): Modified, Size,
Backed Up, the one there now said; Restore (or Return) puts the chosen
one back, asked Keep Both (beside it, named with when it was modified)
or Replace, with a shared lock and its progress; it lists again when a
backup finishes. Checked headless: a file changed loses its tick, gets
it back after Back Up Now; its older version restored beside it.

**Google Drive's setup** (`drive_setup.rs`; Back Up To ▸ Google Drive…;
Ben, 2026-11-07: "we should have each user setup their own desktop app
… have the app walk the user through how to do it"): Google asks each
person to make their own sign-in for an app like this, so the window
walks them through it, a numbered step at a time, each with Open for its
page (Google Cloud's: make a project; turn on the Drive API; set up its
sign-in, Audience Internal for a Google Workspace account, which needs
no publishing and never signs out, External for a Gmail one; add the
`drive.file` scope; publish an External one, which Google now lets only
with a homepage and a privacy-policy address, or it signs it out every
7 days; make a Desktop app client and download its JSON; the agent of
Agent Setup found the publishing rule, 2026-11-08); then the client given (Choose File… for the JSON, or
its ID and secret typed: the secret a password field) and Sign In with
Google: the browser to the consent page (Copy Address if it didn't
open), the answer taken, the folder found or made, the backup there
opened (this computer's key, the keys Passwords keeps) or made, the
sign-in kept in the login keyring (`olo_system::secrets::DISKBACKUP_GOOGLE`)
and the client in Passwords ("DiskBackup Google Client"): on another
computer, Sign In with the One in Passwords skips the steps. 720 points
wide (as DiskBackup's window: its words wrap less, so with every step
shown it's 708 points tall, inside 1280 × 800), and it follows what it
shows (`fixed`).
`--set-up-drive [CLIENT_FILE | ID SECRET]` does the same from the
command line (none: the client Passwords keeps), the consent page's
address printed. For tests, `OLO_DISKBACKUP_GOOGLE_API` is a Google of
our own (no browser opened; the window writes the address to
`$OLO_DISKBACKUP_DIR/sign-in.url`) and `OLO_DISKBACKUP_GOOGLE` the
sign-in; `tests/set_up_drive.rs` runs `--set-up-drive`, plays the
browser, then the service backs up to it (`serve_google`, ignored,
serves the fake for trying the window by hand). The layout review no
longer counts a button's default ring as crowded lines, however wide the
button (`layout_review::crowded_lines`).

DiskBackup's window and the setup window are forms at the size of what
they show, so they float (`WindowOptions::floating`): never zoomed by
Focus or put in a tile (Ben, 2026-11-08: "diskbackup looks silly in focus
mode"). Restore and Versions, browsers of what a backup holds, are
windows like Tracker's.

**Agent Setup** (`agent_setup.rs`; the setup window's Let an Agent Do
It…; Ben, 2026-11-08: "an "Agent Setup" feature to disk backup where an
agent can do the google drive oauth/app setup"): an agent does the steps.
The person chooses the Google account's login from Passwords (its
`Shares` items: those that say Google, else every login; no secrets
read). DiskBackup starts its agent screen (`diskbackup-setup`; `olo-screen
start` unless it's running) and shares the login with it (`SetShares`,
besides what the screen has: `shared_too`). Then it opens a Terminal
window running Claude Code (`olo-terminal -w DIR -e claude …`), with
Preferences ▸ AI's Claude Code model and effort (`AiSettings::claude_code`:
Opus 5.5 on Medium by default). It starts in a folder of its own
(`$XDG_STATE_HOME/olo/diskbackup-agent-setup`, the task kept there as
TASK.md; Claude Code asks once whether to trust it, and the home folder
would be far more than the task needs). It may read the screens'
pictures and ~/Downloads without asking (`--add-dir`), and run `olo-screen`
and the done command (`--allowedTools`); `--no-chrome` keeps it off the
person's own Chrome. The task (`brief`): the screen, how to sign in with
the shared login there without seeing or typing its password (Olo's
Chrome's Autofill with Passwords, or `op … | pbcopy` and ⌘V), the six
steps, and the finish: `olo-diskbackup --agent-setup-done CLIENT_FILE
--screen NAME`, run in the background. That keeps the client in Passwords
("DiskBackup Google Client"), signs DiskBackup in with Google's consent
page opened on the agent's screen (`olo-screen run NAME olo-chrome URL`)
for the agent to allow, sets DiskBackup up (`set_up_drive`), prints how it
went for the agent, and tells DiskBackup's window (forwarded
`--agent-setup-done`), which says it's set up. The person follows along
in Terminal and can talk to the agent there. Tests:
`OLO_DISKBACKUP_AGENT_SCREEN` (another screen), `OLO_DISKBACKUP_AGENT_COMMAND`
(a stand-in for `claude`), `OLO_KEYCHAIN_SOCKET` (a stand-in Passwords),
and `OLO_DISKBACKUP_AGENT_CHECK_ONLY` (the done command stops once
signed in: nothing made in the real Drive with a test's key, which would
clash with the person's own setup later). `tests/set_up_drive.rs`'s
`agent_setup_done` runs the done command against the fake Google and a
stand-in Passwords.

**Restore** (`restore.rs`; File ▸ Restore…, ⌘R, or Restore… beside Back
Up Now): the snapshots newest first; the chosen one's folders browsed as
they were then (Name, Size, Modified; Return or a double-click goes in, Up
goes out; the home folder first); what's selected put back where it was
(asked first if something's there now: Replace, or Keep Both, the restored
one named with its date, "todo (from 7 Nov 2026 20.14).txt") or into a
folder chosen (Restore To…). Opening the backup, reading a folder and
putting back each run on a worker; putting back says its progress every
quarter second and stops at Stop (what was restored so far stays). It
holds a shared lock (waiting, said, while the backup is tidied) and reads
the index again first; browsing reads it again if a folder can't be read
(tidied since the window opened: what moved, found where it went).
Checked headless: a file changed between two snapshots, the older one's
version restored with Keep Both beside the current one, both as they
should be.

Measured (release, one thread, this machine, 2026-11-07;
`tests/round_trip.rs`'s `throughput`, `OLO_DB_SRC` the folder): data/
(988 MB, 12,160 files, pictures mostly) first backed up in 4.8 s
(207 MB/s; 7.5 s, 132 MB/s, before the one buffer and zstd context), 947
MB stored; again with nothing changed 0.03 s, nothing stored. 100,000
small files in 21,041 folders: first 1.13 s (23 s before: an 8 MiB buffer
zeroed for each), unchanged 0.41 s (trees from the cache). Tidying them
(the service, a folder store): nothing to copy, 0.23 s (21,041 trees
walked); with 55% of them deleted, 3 packs copied from (23 MB read, 14 MB
written) in 0.22 s. `round_trip` backs up,
changes (bytes inserted, a file added, one removed), backs up again (1
changed, 1 new, the rest unchanged, under 4 MiB new), restores both
versions and checks nothing in the store is readable.

## Passwords (apps/passwords, crates/onepassword)

**Undo** (undo.rs, `olo_kit::undo`): Edit ▸ Undo and Redo for items
changed (put back as they were), made (deleted) and deleted (made again:
a new item, every field as it was; `Vault::delete` gives back what it
deleted). Each is a save, a creation or a deletion like any other, so a
sync with 1Password takes it as one; the store's jobs carry a `Tag` (what
for, the step's name, an edit's item as it was) that its reply gives
back, and the reply records the step. An item with files attached can't
be made again (its files went), so its Delete still says it's for good;
the Archive isn't undone (nothing takes an item out of it yet). Steps
hold secrets: they go when Passwords locks (and when the store changes).

**Searching**: the toolbar's `SearchField` and a `FilterBar` over the
list (Tag, Has) share one query (`olo_kit::search`). Words find an item
by its title, username, websites, tags, kind, its sections' titles, its
fields' labels (a secret's too), the values of those that aren't secret,
and its notes; with words, the best come first (title 4, username and
site 3, tags 2, the rest 1), else by title; what was found is marked in
each row, whose second line is the username (else the site), or, when
the search found it inside the item, where: "Admin Console › region:
eu-west" (the field with most of the words; `found_in`, worked out with
the list, once per change). The item pane marks it too (section titles,
labels, and values that aren't secret). Filters: `type:` (login,
secure-note…), `vault:`, `tag:`, `site:`, `user:`, `has:` otp, password,
website, files, reused (its password is another item's too), weak (under
12 characters, or of one kind), and `section:` and `field:` (by title or
label, suggested with how many items have each), which narrow the item
pane as well to just those sections and fields (`-section:` and `-field:`
leave them out), saying so under its header. The vault worker sends a
`Searchable` for every item with the list (`store::index`, again after
each change): the username, each field as `FieldText` (its section's
title, its label, its value unless secret), that and the notes as text,
and flags; never a password, code, card number or key, and of a
password only whether it is weak or reused. So searching finds usernames
of items never opened.

**Editing**: the editor shows the fields as the item pane does: the
built-in ones and untitled sections' first, then each titled section
under its heading (one with no fields yet too); each group ends with its
own Add Field…, whose field goes at the end of that section (the first
group's in the untitled section custom fields go in, made when first
needed; `Editor::groups`, `add_field`) and is focused: its label if it
has none yet, else its value. A passkey's section has none.

`crates/onepassword` (package `olo-onepassword`) is a Rust 1Password SDK
modelled on the Go one: the same `Client` (`Secrets`, `Items`, `Vaults`,
`Groups`, `ItemShares`, `ItemFiles`, `Environments`), the same types and
JSON shapes (camelCase, tagged enums), `op://` references, the password
generator (random, memorable from the EFF word list, PIN) and TOTP. It
talks to the 1Password desktop app's SDK integration, as the official SDKs
do, over the abstract unix socket `@1PASSWORD_SDK_INTERGATIONS` (sic): one
connection per call; frames are a u32 LE length (counting the flag byte),
a flag byte (2 = more, 1 = last) and up to 499,999 bytes of a JSON request
`{kind: init_client|invoke|release_client, account_name, payload: base64}`;
the reply is `{success, payload: base64}` whose payload is the result's raw
JSON (or `{name, message}` on failure). 1Password asks the user to allow
each app and unlocks itself; users turn on Settings ▸ Developer ▸ Integrate
with other apps. Service-account (token) access is not implemented: that
needs 1Password's closed core.

`onepassword::accounts::local()` lists the accounts signed in to the
app (name, email, sign-in address, UUID) from the summaries in its
`1password.sqlite` (`~/.config/1Password`, or the Flatpak's;
`OLO_1PASSWORD_DATA` overrides), read-only and nothing else from it.
Passwords' setup offers them as a choice and keeps the UUID, which the
SDK integration takes as the account's name.

Tests never touch the real app. `onepassword-fake [--account NAME]
[--socket NAME] [--data FILE] [--accounts DIR] [--items N]` (DIR gets a
`1password.sqlite` listing it) serves an in-memory account (two vaults of
sample items, item versions, OTP codes; `--items N` adds N made-up
logins, to measure Passwords with a vault the size of a person's) over
the same protocol;
`tests/desktop.rs` drives it. Apps take `OLO_1PASSWORD_SOCKET` to use it.

Passwords is the app: sources (vaults, categories, Archive), a two-line
item list and the selected item's fields (hover for Copy/Show; one-time
codes count down), an editor with templates per category, a Password
Generator panel, and File/Edit/Item/View menus (⌘C username, ⇧⌘C password,
⇧⌘O one-time code, ⌘0 All Items, ⌘1–⌘9 the vaults by place, as
`app_keys` has them). Secrets go to the clipboard with
`olo_kit::copy::secret` and leave after `clear_seconds` (quit before,
Passwords runs on without its windows until they do: `Passwords::quit`
closes them and ends at the next thing due, the secret's time; opened
meanwhile, it carries on). A field (or website) drags out as text onto
another app's field (`Detail::drag`, what goes `Passwords::dragged_field`:
a one-time password's current code;
the picture shows the field's name, never the value). It opens locked and locks after
`lock_minutes` idle, and when the screen locks if `lock_with_screen`
(`lock.rs`): Touch ID through fprintd, claimed only
while the locked window has the keyboard, or the account password through
PAM. Those, and `auto_sync`, are Preferences ▸ Security's
(`Settings::security.passwords`, followed live through
`olo_kit::settings::watch`; the screen locking comes from
`settings::watch_power`, `PowerStatus::locked`; View ▸ Lock After writes
the same setting with `settings::update`). Its own settings (accounts,
the generator) live in `passwords.json`.

It is on olo-kit. Passwords runs with no window (started at login as
the SSH agent and the keychain, locked) and its window comes and goes,
so its state and what it does are the app's, not a window's: one
`Passwords` behind a lock (`app()`, `main.rs`). The app's looper takes
what the proxy brings (the store's replies, the lock's, other
programs' requests, settings) with `Passwords::message`; each window's
view locks it while it says what it shows and again to act, and
`Passwords::changed` tells the windows to say what they show again.
Nothing that waits is done under the lock, and nothing calls `app()`
while holding it (it isn't re-entrant: a handler takes what it needs,
lets go, then calls the kit). What only a window has (its text fields,
its list, its scrollers) is its view's; what the app wants of those
(the password field emptied, the search field given the keyboard, the
editor's form made again for fields that came or went) it leaves in
`Ui`, which the views take as they next say what they show
(`take_asks`). The main window is `view::MainView` (the setup, lock and
connection panels; the toolbar, sources, items under their filters and
the status line); the selected item or its editor is a view of its own,
`view::Detail`, so a one-time code counting down (the pane says what
it shows again on the second, only while one shows), the pointer
moving over the fields and typing in the editor draw that pane alone.
Nothing ticks: the app's looper keeps one timer for the next thing due
(a sync, the auto-lock, the status line clearing, a copied secret's
time when it's closing), set again whenever the app changes
(`next_due` lists only what `tick` would act on, so a time gone by
never spins), and the main window one for when "Synced a minute ago"
next reads differently. The list is worked out once for each change to
the items, the source or the search (`visible`), and its rows keep
their drawing by what they show (`row_key`). Review Sync, Sync
Problems, the generator (a panel: it floats, never a tab) and the
passkey question are views in windows of their own that read the app;
alerts are the app's (`open_app_alert`, answered on the alert's
looper); a passkey question closes itself when the page gives up.
Debug builds only take the PAM test
service, so a release build can't be unlocked in a test session: to
measure one, build it with `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_DEBUG_ASSERTIONS=true`
in a scratch `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`. Tests give it a keychain socket of its
own (`OLO_KEYCHAIN_SOCKET`; the default is the person's Passwords') and
a fake 1Password on a socket of its own (`onepassword-fake --socket
NAME --accounts DIR`, `OLO_1PASSWORD_SOCKET=NAME`,
`OLO_1PASSWORD_DATA=DIR`). `olo-keychain-ask` (an example of
olo-keychain: `cargo build -p olo-keychain --example olo-keychain-ask`)
asks a test's Passwords one thing as Chrome's extension would (a
passkey to make or sign with) and prints the answer's kind alone; it
wants `OLO_KEYCHAIN_SOCKET`, so it never reaches the person's.
A test session keeps what its Passwords kept (its dir's `config`), so a
second start is a locked one; remove `config/olo/passwords.*` and
`passwords.key` for the setup again. Return on the item list opens the
item's website in a browser: tests press it only with an alert up.

**Its own store** (`vault.rs`). Every vault and item lives on this
computer, so the app, Chrome's extension and the palette never wait on
1Password: `passwords.vault` in the config directory, "TABV", a format
byte, a 24-byte nonce and the JSON sealed with XChaCha20-Poly1305 (header
as associated data), written whole and atomically (0600) after each
change. The key is 32 random bytes in the login keyring
(`olo_system::secrets`, a Secret Service client that first checks a
keyring owns, or can start, `org.freedesktop.secrets`, so with none it
answers "nothing" at once; the session bus's calls time out after 10 s;
PAM unlocks the
keyring at login, so Touch ID still opens Passwords). A store whose key is
missing is never overwritten with a new one. `OLO_PASSWORDS_KEYFILE`
keeps the key in a file instead; tsession sets it for every session, so
test apps never touch the real keyring. The worker (`store.rs`) owns the
store: it opens it at the unlock, lets it go at the lock (after a running
sync), and answers the UI, Chrome's extension and op from it. Items keep 1Password's
types; each entry also records what 1Password last had (version, update
time, archive state), whether it changed here, and a revision; deletions
of synced items leave tombstones. Without an account (Keep Only on This
Computer) items live in a local "Personal" vault.

**Syncing with 1Password** (`sync.rs`, optional: the setup panel or File ▸
1Password Accounts…) never changes anything, on either side, without the
person's approval. It runs in two steps, each on its own thread:

* `sync::plan`, from a snapshot (`Vault::snapshot` changes nothing, even
  for an account switch), only reads. Down: vaults whose
  `content_version` moved are listed (both states); new or changed items
  (update time or state) are fetched fifty at a time with `get_all`;
  items gone there are noted. 1Password refuses to give apps archived
  items ("item is not in an active state"), and one archived id fails a
  whole `get_all`, so only active items are fetched: an item archived
  there since is archived here from its listing (`Change::Archived`),
  archived items never synced are left out with a note, and whatever a
  batch didn't bring is fetched one at a time, so a bad item costs only
  itself. A field 1Password's SDK names but won't give the value of (its
  `Unsupported`, with no value and no section: an older card's expiry,
  three of Ben's cards) is asked for by its secret reference
  (`op://vault/item/field`, `resolve_unread`, all of a batch at once,
  else one by one), which 1Password answers: a card's expiry or
  valid-from that reads as a month and year becomes a `MonthYear`
  ("MM/YYYY"); any other keeps its value. An item synced before that
  with such a field empty is fetched again, once, its vault changed or
  not (`has_unread`). `cargo run -p olo-onepassword --example
  card_shapes [VAULT ITEM]` shows what the 1Password app gives for each
  card (or one item): every field's id, label, type and section, and its
  value's shape only ("NN/NNNN"), never a value or a title, and how its
  unsupported fields resolve. Up: 1Password's copies of items changed here
  are fetched to compare (their unread fields asked for the same way). The plan is the store's `Change`s, what to send,
  and a `Row` for every change either side would see (add, change with the
  parts that differ by name, never values, archive, delete, keep both).
* The store keeps the plan and the UI shows its rows in Review Sync. Only
  `Job::Approve` with that plan's id runs `sync::apply`, which makes
  exactly those changes. A changed item is put against the version that
  was reviewed, and a deletion checks it first, so anything changed in
  1Password meanwhile is refused (reported) rather than overwritten, and
  comes up in the next review. A plan nobody would notice (nothing but
  what was looked at) applies without asking.

With `auto_sync` (the default), plans are made at the unlock, every 5 minutes, 3 s after a change here
(the status line then says "3 sync changes to review"; a click opens
them), and on File ▸ Sync Now or the setup panel's Sync (the review opens
at once). Automatic plans wait while Review Sync is open. Cancel leaves
"Not synced: changes not applied". Changed on both sides: 1Password's copy
stays as the item and ours is kept beside it as "… (conflict)", to be
reviewed next time. A push that lands after another edit here keeps the
edit pending (revisions). The first sync with an account brings in
everything; local-only items move to its Personal (or first) vault.

**Several accounts.** The setup ticks any of the 1Password app's accounts
(`Settings::accounts`, `Linked { id, label }`; the first takes items made
here; an id is the UUID, or a name typed by hand, which the app also
answers to and which is kept). The store keeps which account each vault is
in (`Data::vault_account`); `Vault::snapshot(account, home)` holds only that
account's vaults (and, for the first, the local vault), so one account
never sees another's vaults as gone. `Job::Sync { accounts }` plans each
in turn into one `Plan` of per-account parts, one review: with more than
one account a vault is named "Personal (Work)" there, in problems, the
editor and the item's header, and the sidebar lists each account's vaults
under its name (as Tracker lists volumes). An account that can't be
reached is a problem, not a failure, unless none can be. Unticking one
asks first, then `Job::RemoveAccount` drops its vaults and items here
(never-sent items stay, in the local vault). Stores and settings from the
one-account days carry over (`Data::account`, `Settings::account`). The
fake serves more signed-in accounts on one socket (`FakeAccount::others`). Files attached in 1Password aren't copied (their metadata
is), so they aren't shown.

**Problems** are `sync::Problem`s (vault, item or none, a reason in plain
words from `sync::reason`, and whether it's only a note), never joined
text. The status line counts them ("Synced just now · 2 problems", red
only for failures); the review shows one line ("⚠ 2 problems reading
1Password…"). Either opens Sync Problems: grouped by vault
(`sync::grouped`, repeats dropped), a warning or info icon, the item and
its reason under it, with Copy (`sync::as_text`) and Sync Again. The fake
behaves as 1Password does: archived items can't be read, and a vault with
`"no_access": true` can't be listed.
